title: Germs, medicines and vaccines: how the body and medicine meet an infection

summary.text: Two children both have a sore throat. The doctor gives one of them tablets and sends the other home with warm water and rest. The doctor is not being unfair. Tablets that kill bacteria do nothing to viruses, and most sore throats are caused by viruses. Your child finds out what a medicine really does by testing which kitchen things stop a living microbe, and by playing a game in which a medicine leaves a few tough germs behind. Then they learn how a vaccine shows the body a safe picture of a germ, so that the body is ready, and why one vaccinated child protects the child sitting next to her.
summary.art: A doctor's table with two children: one holding a strip of tablets, the other holding a cup of warm water, and above them a small drawing of a bacterium and a virus.

intro.hook: A boy in your class had measles last year. You have never had measles, and you did not catch it, even though you sat in the same room. Something in your body was ready for the germ before the germ arrived. What was it, and who put it there?
intro.text: In this unit you find out what happens inside a body when germs get in, and what medicines can and cannot do. You test which kitchen things slow down a living microbe. You play a game with rice and dal in which a medicine leaves a few tough germs behind, and see what those survivors do next. And you learn, in plain words, how a vaccine works and why it protects people who never had it.
intro.art: A child's arm with a small round plaster on it, and beside the arm a faint drawing of the same arm with tiny defenders standing guard in the blood.

outcomes: I can sort illnesses by their cause, which may be bacteria, a virus, a fungus, a parasite or no germ at all, and say which ones pass from person to person.
I can describe what happens in a body from the time germs get in to the time the person feels ill, and say what a fever is for.
I can say what the body's defenders do, and why the body is faster the second time it meets a germ.
I can explain why an antibiotic works on bacteria but not on viruses, and say what other kinds of medicine are for.
I can explain, from the rice and dal game, how germs that survive a medicine become common.
I can say when a medicine is needed and when it is not, and name the danger signs that need a doctor at once.
I can explain in simple words how a vaccine works, and why it holds no working germ.
I can explain why a vaccinated person also protects people who cannot be vaccinated.

terms.meaning: An illness caused by a germ that has got into the body. Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites can all cause one.
terms.example: Typhoid is an infectious disease caused by bacteria. A broken arm is not infectious, because no germ causes a broken arm.
terms.art: Two columns of small pictures: a child with a rash and a child with a cough under 'germ', and a child with a plaster on an arm under 'no germ'.

terms.meaning: The time between germs getting in and the first signs of illness. The germs are multiplying quietly in that time.
terms.example: For a cold the incubation period is about one to three days. For measles it is about ten to fourteen days.
terms.art: A calendar strip with a germ landing on day 1, a quiet row of days with a tiny growing crowd, and a sneezing child on day 12.

terms.meaning: A body temperature higher than usual, about 38 degrees Celsius or more. The brain raises the temperature while the body fights an infection.
terms.example: A child with flu may have a fever and feel shivery as the temperature goes up.
terms.art: A digital thermometer reading 38.6 beside a child in bed with a damp cloth on her forehead.

terms.meaning: The parts of the body that find and remove germs. They include skin, tears, stomach acid and many kinds of white blood cell.
terms.example: Your immune system clears most colds in about a week without any medicine.
terms.art: A child drawn as an outline with small guards at the skin, nose and mouth, and patrol cells moving through the blood.

terms.meaning: A tiny protein that the body makes to fit one particular germ, the way a key fits one lock. It sticks to the germ and marks them to be removed.
terms.example: After measles, your blood holds antibodies that fit the measles virus and no other germ.
terms.art: Small Y-shaped antibodies attached to the knobbly surface of a germ, each fitting a knob like a key in a lock.

terms.meaning: A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them multiplying. It does nothing to viruses.
terms.example: A doctor may give an antibiotic for a bacterial throat infection but not for a cold.
terms.art: A strip of tablets with an arrow pointing to a crossed-out bacterium, and a virus left alone next to the cross.

terms.meaning: A medicine that slows down one kind of virus from making copies. Each antiviral works on only a few viruses.
terms.example: Some doctors give an antiviral to people who are at risk of getting very ill from flu.
terms.art: A virus inside a cell with a small barrier placed in front of the copying machinery of the cell.

terms.meaning: A liquid or cream put on skin to kill germs on the surface, for example on a cut. It is not safe to swallow.
terms.example: A grown-up cleans a scrape with an antiseptic or with soap and water.
terms.art: A grown-up's hand dabbing a scrape on a child's knee with a cotton ball and a small bottle.

terms.meaning: A germ is resistant to a medicine when the medicine no longer kills them. The germ is resistant, not the person.
terms.example: Resistant bacteria can carry on multiplying in a body that is taking an antibiotic.
terms.art: A crowd of bacteria with most crossed out by a tablet and a few standing untouched at the edge.

terms.meaning: The amount of a medicine to take at one time. A child's dose usually depends on how much the child weighs.
terms.example: A label may say 5 millilitres, three times a day. Too little may not work and too much can harm.
terms.art: A small measuring spoon of syrup next to the bottle label that shows the dose and the times.

terms.meaning: A paper or message from a doctor that says which medicine to take, how much and for how long.
terms.example: The pharmacist gave the antibiotic only after seeing the doctor's prescription.
terms.art: A doctor's handwritten note with a stethoscope beside it, and a hand passing it across a pharmacy counter.

terms.meaning: An effect of a medicine that you did not want, such as a rash or a loose tummy. Most are mild.
terms.example: An antibiotic can upset the helpful bacteria in the gut and cause loose motions.
terms.art: A child holding her tummy beside a tablet, with a small label 'not the reason we took it'.

terms.meaning: A drink of clean water with the right amounts of salt and sugar. It replaces the water and salts the body loses in loose motions.
terms.example: A packet of ORS mixed in clean water is given in small sips to a child with loose motions.
terms.art: A steel tumbler of ORS with a packet beside it, and a child taking small sips from a spoon.

terms.meaning: A safe version of a germ, or a piece of one, given so the body learns to recognise the real germ. A vaccine does not give you the illness.
terms.example: The measles vaccine teaches the body to make antibodies against the measles virus.
terms.art: A small vial and syringe on one side, and on the other a child's blood with antibodies already waiting.

terms.meaning: Being protected from a germ because the body is ready for them. Immunity can come from a vaccine or from having had the illness.
terms.example: After chickenpox, most people have immunity for life.
terms.art: A child with a shield made of antibodies, a germ bouncing off.

terms.meaning: An extra dose of a vaccine given later, to remind the body and keep the protection strong.
terms.example: A booster against tetanus and diphtheria is given at school age in India.
terms.art: A timeline with a first dose, a gap, and a second dose arrow lifting a falling line of protection back up.

terms.meaning: When enough people in a group are protected, a germ cannot find enough people to spread to, so even people who are not protected are safer.
terms.example: A baby too young for the measles vaccine is safer when everyone around the baby is vaccinated.
terms.art: A ring of vaccinated children around a baby in the middle, with an arrow from a germ bouncing off the ring.

terms.meaning: To remove a disease from the whole world, so that nobody gets it anywhere. Smallpox is the only human disease eradicated so far.
terms.art: A globe with red dots fading to none across a row of four pictures.

terms.meaning: An outbreak of an illness that spreads across many countries or the whole world.
terms.example: Covid-19 was a pandemic that began in 2019 and reached every continent.
terms.art: A world map with small red dots on every continent.

explanations.concept: Which illnesses come from germs, and which do not
explanations.context: This card sorts illnesses by their cause, because the cause decides which medicine can help.
explanations.definition: An infectious disease is an illness caused by a germ that has got into the body. Some infectious diseases pass from person to person, and some do not.
explanations.description: Different germs cause different illnesses. Bacteria cause typhoid, tuberculosis and many throat infections. Viruses cause colds, flu, measles, dengue and chickenpox. A fungus causes ringworm. A parasite causes malaria. All of these are infectious diseases, because a germ gets in. Some illnesses have no germ at all. A broken bone comes from a fall. Diabetes comes from the way the body handles sugar. Anaemia often comes from too little iron in food. Nobody can catch these from a friend. Contagious is a smaller group, the infectious diseases that pass from person to person. Tetanus is infectious, because bacteria from soil get into a deep cut, but nobody catches tetanus from another person. Knowing the cause tells you what to do. Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites each need a different kind of medicine, and an illness with no germ needs none of them.
examples: Measles is infectious and very contagious, because the virus travels in the air.
Tetanus is infectious but not contagious. The bacteria live in soil and get into deep cuts.
Diabetes is not infectious. No germ causes diabetes, so nobody catches the illness from a friend.
explanations.art: A table with five columns headed bacteria, virus, fungus, parasite and no germ, with a small picture of an illness in each.

explanations.concept: Inside you: from landing to feeling ill
explanations.context: This card follows an infection through a body, day by day, and says what a fever is for.
explanations.definition: The time between germs getting in and the first sign of illness is the incubation period. During it the germs are multiplying, and the body is getting ready.
explanations.description: Think of a cold virus that lands in your nose on Monday. For the first day or so you feel perfectly well. Inside, the virus is entering cells and making copies, and each new copy enters another cell. Your body notices. Cells that are being attacked send out chemical alarm signals, and defenders hurry to the nose. Those signals are also what make you feel unwell. They tell the brain to raise the body's temperature by a degree or two, which is a fever, and they make you tired. Many of the signs of illness are signs of the fight, not of the germ. The incubation period is different for each germ. For a cold it is about one to three days. For flu it is about one to four days. For measles it is about ten to fourteen days, and for chickenpox about two weeks. After the fight, most people get better because the defenders have cleared the germs away.
examples: A runny nose is partly your body washing germs out of the nose with extra mucus.
A child with measles may feel well for a week and a half after catching the virus, and can pass it on in the last days of that time.
Feeling very tired during an infection is the body slowing you down while it uses energy for the fight.
explanations.art: A calendar strip, five days wide: germs landing on Monday, a quiet crowd growing on Tuesday and Wednesday, alarm signals on Thursday and a child in bed with a thermometer on Friday.

explanations.concept: The body's defenders: walls, patrols and memory
explanations.context: This card says how the body clears germs, and why it is quicker the second time. Vaccines depend on this.
explanations.definition: The immune system is the set of parts that find and remove germs. Its first part is a set of walls. Its second part is a set of defenders that learn.
explanations.description: The walls come first. Skin, tears, mucus in the nose, and the acid in the stomach stop most germs. A germ that gets past the walls meets patrol cells, which are kinds of white blood cell. Some patrol cells swallow germs whole. Other white blood cells make antibodies. An antibody is a tiny protein with a shape that fits one particular germ, the way a key fits one lock. The antibody sticks to the germ and marks them, so that the patrol cells can find and remove them. The first time the body meets a germ, making enough of the right antibodies takes about a week or two. That is why you can be ill for days. After the fight, some of the white blood cells stay on for years, ready to make the same antibody quickly. These are memory cells. The second time the same germ arrives, the body may clear them in a day or two, often before you feel anything.
examples: After chickenpox, memory cells stay in your blood for many years, so most people never get chickenpox twice.
A cut that gets dirty still heals, because patrol cells swallow the bacteria that got in.
An antibody for the measles virus does nothing against the mumps virus, because the shape does not fit.
explanations.art: Three panels: walls at skin and nose, patrol cells swallowing a germ, and Y-shaped antibodies fitting the knobs of a germ like keys, with memory cells waiting at the side.

explanations.concept: What medicines do, and what they do not do
explanations.context: This card sorts medicines by what they do, because people often think every medicine kills germs.
explanations.definition: A medicine is a substance taken to prevent, treat or ease an illness. Some medicines act on the germ. Others act on the body.
explanations.description: There are four jobs a medicine can do. Some medicines kill germs or stop them multiplying. Antibiotics do this for bacteria. Antivirals do it for a few viruses. Antifungal medicines do it for fungi. Other medicines ease the signs, and do nothing to the germ. Paracetamol, for example, lowers a fever and eases pain, so a child can rest. A third kind replaces what the body has lost. In loose motions the body loses water and salts, and the drink called ORS puts them back. A fourth kind prevents illness, and that is a vaccine. A doctor chooses by cause. For a throat infection caused by bacteria, an antibiotic may help. For most colds, which are caused by viruses, no medicine kills the virus, and the best treatment is rest and drinks while the defenders do the work. For most loose motions in children, ORS is the main treatment, and a doctor may add zinc tablets.
examples: An antibiotic helps with a bacterial throat infection but has no effect on a cold.
Paracetamol lowers a fever. The fever was a sign of the fight, so the infection is still there.
ORS does not kill the germ that caused the loose motions. It keeps the body from drying out until the body clears the germ.
explanations.art: Four small pictures in a row: a tablet hitting a germ, a thermometer going down, a glass of ORS refilling a tired child, and a vaccine in an arm.

explanations.concept: Why an antibiotic hits bacteria and leaves you alone
explanations.context: This card says how antibiotics work, and why they cannot work on a virus.
explanations.definition: An antibiotic works by stopping something that bacteria need and that human cells do not have.
explanations.description: A bacterium is a single cell with a tough wall around the outside. To grow and split, she must keep building that wall. Penicillin stops the building. The wall weakens, and the bacterium bursts. Human cells have no wall, so penicillin has nothing to hit in us. Other antibiotics block the tiny machines inside a bacterium that build proteins. Those machines have a different shape from ours, so the medicine fits theirs and not ours. A virus is different again. A virus is not a cell, has no wall and no machines of their own. They make copies only by taking over a cell that belongs to someone else. So an antibiotic has nothing to attack in a virus. That is also why an antiviral is hard to make. It must stop a virus without stopping the cell the virus is using. Antibiotics are not perfect. They also kill some of the helpful bacteria in the gut, which is why they sometimes cause loose motions.
examples: Penicillin makes the wall of a bacterium weak, so the bacterium bursts as she grows.
A cold virus has no wall, so penicillin has nothing to attack.
Taking an antibiotic can cause loose motions because helpful gut bacteria are killed along with the harmful ones.
explanations.art: A bacterium with a thick wall bursting after a tablet, beside a human cell with no wall untouched and a virus with no wall either.

explanations.context: This card tells where some well-known medicines came from, and who found them.
explanations.definition: Many medicines were found in living beings, such as trees, moulds and soil bacteria, and then made in factories.
explanations.description: Living beings have been fighting each other with chemicals for a very long time. Moulds and soil bacteria make substances that kill other microbes near them, and some of those became our antibiotics. In 1928, Alexander Fleming saw a clear ring around a mould on a dish of bacteria, where no bacteria grew. That mould made penicillin. It took more than ten years, and the work of Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and Norman Heatley, before penicillin was made in enough quantity for patients. Dorothy Hodgkin worked out the shape of the penicillin molecule in the 1940s. In 1943, a mouldy cantaloupe from a market in Peoria, in the United States, gave scientists a mould that, grown in big tanks, made far more penicillin than Fleming's mould. The story says a lab worker called Mary Hunt brought the fruit in, though the records are not certain. Streptomycin, the first medicine for tuberculosis, came from a soil bacterium, and a graduate student named Albert Schatz was the one who found it. Quinine, a medicine for malaria, came from the bark of the cinchona tree. In 1972, Tu Youyou, a Chinese scientist, found artemisinin in a plant called sweet wormwood, after reading a fourth century book of remedies. She won a Nobel Prize in 2015. In 1950, two American scientists made nystatin, the first safe medicine against fungus infections. They were Elizabeth Lee Hazen and Rachel Fuller Brown, and they worked in different cities and posted samples to each other.
examples: Penicillin comes from a mould that is closely related to the green mould on old bread.
Quinine comes from cinchona bark, and cinchona trees were once grown in the Nilgiri hills to make it.
Artemisinin comes from sweet wormwood, a plant used in China for fever for many centuries.
explanations.art: Four small pictures: a dish with a clear ring around a green mould, a cinchona branch, a sweet wormwood plant, and a mouldy cantaloupe on a lab bench.

explanations.context: This card explains why a medicine that works today can stop working, using the game you played with rice and dal.
explanations.definition: Resistance appears when a few germs survive a medicine, multiply, and become the new crowd. The germ becomes resistant. The person does not.
explanations.description: Bacteria multiply by splitting in two, and each time they copy their genes, a tiny mistake can creep in. Most mistakes change nothing. A very few help the bacterium to survive a medicine, for example by making a chemical that breaks the medicine down. So in a crowd of billions of bacteria, a few may already be tough before any medicine arrives. When a person takes an antibiotic, the ordinary bacteria die. The tough few are left, with plenty of food and room, and they multiply. After a few days, nearly all the bacteria in the body are tough. Bacteria can also hand pieces of their genes to each other, even to bacteria of other kinds, so a tough gene can spread fast. This is natural selection, the same process that shaped every living being. The medicine does not teach the bacteria anything. It only chooses which ones carry on. The more an antibiotic is used, the more chances tough bacteria have. Doctors call this a world-wide problem. A study published in 2022 estimated that more than a million people died in 2019 as a direct result of infections that medicines could not treat.
examples: A person does not become resistant. The bacteria in their body become resistant.
In the rice and dal game, the medicine removed most of the rice, and the dal grains multiplied in the space that was left.
A bacterium can pass a tough gene to a different kind of bacterium, so resistance can jump between kinds.
explanations.art: Four panels: a mixed crowd of bacteria, a tablet removing most of them, a few tough ones left, and the same few multiplied into a new crowd.

explanations.concept: When to use a medicine, and when not
explanations.context: This card gives plain rules for medicines at home, and says when a child needs a doctor.
explanations.definition: A medicine helps only when it is the right one for the cause, in the right dose, for the right time. A medicine taken for the wrong reason can do harm and no good.
explanations.description: Here are the rules that doctors give families. Give a medicine only when a doctor or a health worker has said so, and follow the dose and times on the label. A child's dose depends on weight, so never guess. Do not give a child a medicine that was bought for someone else, and do not save left-over tablets for next time. Check the date on the packet, and keep all medicines out of reach of small children. Do not press a doctor for an antibiotic for a cold. For most colds and coughs, rest, warm drinks and time are the treatment. Ask the doctor when to stop a medicine, because the right length depends on the illness. Some signs mean a child needs a doctor at once. The signs are these. A child cannot drink, vomits everything, has a fit, is very sleepy and hard to wake, or has trouble breathing. A fever that lasts more than two or three days also needs a doctor. This card is general advice. A doctor who knows the child knows best.
examples: A child with a cold and a runny nose needs rest and drinks, not an antibiotic.
A child who cannot keep any drink down needs a doctor the same day.
Left-over tablets from last month's illness should not be given for a new illness without asking a doctor.
explanations.art: A kitchen shelf with a medicine box on a high shelf, a label showing a dose, a calendar showing the expiry date and a phone with a doctor's number.

explanations.context: This card says what a vaccine is and how it works.
explanations.definition: A vaccine shows the body a safe version of a germ, so the body learns to fight the real germ before the real germ arrives.
explanations.description: A vaccine does not contain a working, full-strength germ that can make you ill. It contains something that looks like the germ to the defenders. There are several kinds. Some contain a germ that has been killed. Some contain a germ that has been weakened so much that the germ can barely multiply. Some contain just one piece of the germ, such as a part of the coat. For tetanus, the vaccine holds a harmless form of the poison the bacteria make. A few newer vaccines hold a set of instructions for the body's own cells to make one harmless piece of the germ for a short time. In every kind, the defenders see the piece, make antibodies, and keep memory cells. If the real germ arrives months or years later, the body is ready, and often the germ is cleared before there is any illness. Some vaccines are given once, some need two or three doses, and some need a booster. Common side effects are a sore arm and a mild fever for a day. Serious reactions are very rare, and health services watch for them. Katalin Karikó, a biochemist born in Hungary, found how to change a set of instructions so that the body does not attack them, which made the newer vaccines possible. She and Drew Weissman shared the Nobel Prize in 2023. Rabies is a special case. The virus takes weeks to travel from a bite to the brain, so the vaccine can be given after a bite and still teach the body in time.
examples: The tetanus vaccine holds a harmless form of the poison that tetanus bacteria make.
The measles vaccine holds a weakened measles virus that barely multiplies.
A person bitten by a dog that might have rabies is given the vaccine at once, as the virus is still on the way.
explanations.art: A vaccine vial with four small labelled pictures floating out of it: a killed germ, a weakened germ, a piece of the coat and a harmless form of a poison.

explanations.concept: Herd protection: how vaccinated people protect others
explanations.context: This card connects vaccines to the germ chains you studied in Level 3, and to the Ring the Germ game.
explanations.definition: Herd protection means that when most people in a group are protected against a germ, the germ rarely finds anyone to pass to, so people who are not protected are safer too.
explanations.description: Every germ chain needs a next person. A vaccinated person is a broken link. If most of the people around a germ are vaccinated, the germ keeps meeting broken links, and the chain dies out. This protects babies who are too young for a vaccine, and people whose bodies cannot take it, for example those having cancer treatment. How many people need to be protected depends on the germ. Measles is one of the most contagious illnesses known. One ill child can pass it to twelve to eighteen others who are not protected. So about 95 out of every 100 people need protection to stop measles spreading. Herd protection is not a promise, because it works only while enough people stay vaccinated. When vaccination falls in a place, measles comes back there. In the Ring the Germ game, you saw this. When most houses were vaccinated, the illness stayed small. When only a third were, it spread far.
examples: A baby of five months cannot yet have the measles vaccine, but she is safer when her brothers, cousins and neighbours have had it.
A school where almost every child is vaccinated rarely has a measles outbreak, even if one ill child comes in.
A health worker who finds one case vaccinates the people around the ill person, which cuts the chain.
explanations.art: A square of houses where most are shaded as vaccinated and a few are not, and a germ arrow from one ill house stopped by the shaded houses around.

explanations.context: This card tells where vaccines came from, from a village trick to the end of smallpox.
explanations.definition: People learned to protect each other from illness long before anyone knew what a germ was.
explanations.description: Smallpox was an illness that killed about three in every ten people who caught it. In several countries, people noticed that someone who had survived smallpox never caught it again. So healers scratched a little material from a smallpox sore into the skin of a healthy person, who then usually had a mild illness and was protected. This was called variolation. It sometimes killed the person. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu saw it done in Istanbul, and in 1721 she had her young daughter protected in London, and she told other people. In England in 1774 a farmer called Benjamin Jesty protected his family with matter from cowpox, a mild illness of cows. In 1796, Edward Jenner tested the same idea carefully. A milkmaid called Sarah Nelmes had cowpox sores, and Jenner used matter from one sore on a boy named James Phipps. Later he showed that James did not catch smallpox. In the 1880s, Louis Pasteur made a vaccine for rabies. In 1897, Waldemar Haffkine made a vaccine for plague in Bombay and tested it first on himself. In the 1960s and 1970s, a world campaign found every case of smallpox and vaccinated everyone around it. The last natural case was in 1977, and in 1980 the world was declared free of smallpox. India reported its last case in 1975. India's last case of polio was reported in January 2011, in a girl in West Bengal, and in 2014 the region was declared free of polio. In India, Gagandeep Kang, a doctor and scientist who worked in Vellore, helped test Rotavac. Rotavac is a rotavirus vaccine made in India, and it protects babies from a common cause of dangerous loose motions.
examples: Jesty, Jenner and the milkmaids who knew cowpox all played a part. Jenner's careful test is the one the world remembers.
Haffkine's plague vaccine was tested first on himself, and the institute in Mumbai now carries his name.
The smallpox vaccine protected people so well that smallpox is the only human disease the world has wiped out.
explanations.art: A row of five small pictures: a healer scratching an arm, a milkmaid with a cow, a doctor holding up a vial, a lab flask and a health worker with a bicycle and a cloth bag.

explanations.concept: Boosters and yearly shots: why some protection fades
explanations.context: This card says why some vaccines last for life and others need to be repeated.
explanations.definition: A vaccine can stop working as well over time, or because the germ has changed. A booster or a new vaccine fixes the problem.
explanations.description: Memory cells last longer for some germs than for others. After two doses of the measles vaccine, protection usually lasts a lifetime. Protection against tetanus and diphtheria fades over some years, so a booster is given, as it is to ten-year-olds in India. Another reason is that some germs change. Flu viruses change a little every year, so last year's antibodies may not fit this year's virus, as an old key may not fit a new lock. So scientists study the flu viruses going around every year, and each year's flu vaccine is made to match. Some germs are hard to make a vaccine for, because they change fast or hide from defenders. There is no vaccine yet for the common cold, which is caused by hundreds of kinds of virus. In 2021 and 2023, the World Health Organization recommended the first two vaccines against malaria, for children in places where malaria is common.
examples: A tetanus booster tops up the memory cells that fade over the years.
A flu vaccine is updated each year to match the viruses that are going around.
There is no single vaccine for the common cold, because hundreds of different viruses can cause one.
explanations.art: A falling line labelled protection with arrows lifting it back up at the booster points, beside a key that no longer fits a changed lock.

explanations.concept: How long should a course of antibiotics be?
explanations.context: This card is about a real argument among doctors, so that you see how scientists disagree.
explanations.description: For many years, doctors told patients to finish every tablet in the packet, even after they felt well. The reason given was that stopping early lets the tough bacteria survive and multiply. In 2017, a group of doctors and scientists wrote that there was little evidence for this rule. They said that the longer a person takes an antibiotic, the more chances there are for resistant bacteria to appear in the body. Other doctors replied that for some infections, such as tuberculosis, stopping early is dangerous. Both sides agree on one thing: families should not decide the length of a course themselves, and the doctor who prescribed it should say when to stop.
examples: For tuberculosis, a course of many months is needed, and stopping early is dangerous.
For some urinary and chest infections, studies have found that shorter courses worked as well as longer ones.

perspectives.who: Martin Llewelyn and colleagues, who wrote in the British Medical Journal in 2017
perspectives.explanation: The idea that you must always finish the packet has little evidence behind it. Taking a medicine for longer than needed gives resistant bacteria more chances to appear. Courses should be as short as works, and doctors should say when to stop.
For some illnesses, like tuberculosis and some bone infections, a long course is needed to kill every bacterium, and stopping early is dangerous. The right length depends on the illness.
Follow the doctor's advice exactly, and ask when to stop. Never keep tablets for next time and never stop or extend a course on your own.

explanations.art: A strip of tablets with a calendar behind it, a question mark above, and two doctors on either side pointing to different numbers of days.

explanations.context: This card is about an idea from the edge of science: viruses that kill bacteria, and might one day replace some antibiotics.
explanations.definition: A bacteriophage, or phage, is a virus that attacks only bacteria. Phages are the most common living things on Earth.
explanations.description: A phage lands on one kind of bacterium, pushes in their genes, and makes the bacterium build many new phages. Then the bacterium bursts. In 1896, Ernest Hankin, a British scientist working in Agra, reported that the water of the Ganga and the Yamuna killed cholera bacteria. He also reported that boiling the water removed this power. That is an early sign of phages. In 1915 Frederick Twort in England and in 1917 Felix d'Herelle in France both described them. D'Herelle named them. A phage is very choosy and attacks only one kind of bacterium, and does not hurt people. Doctors in Georgia have used phages to treat infections for about a hundred years, and scientists elsewhere are testing them now for infections that no antibiotic can cure. Nobody yet knows whether phages will work widely, because bacteria can become resistant to phages too, and testing them takes a long time.
examples: A phage that attacks the bacteria of cholera does not touch the bacteria of tuberculosis.
Phage treatment is already used in some hospitals for infections that no antibiotic can cure, under special rules.

agreed.text: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them multiplying. They do nothing to viruses.
agreed.evidence: Antibiotics attack parts that bacteria have and viruses do not, such as a cell wall. Careful trials found that antibiotics do not shorten colds or flu.

agreed.text: Germs that survive a medicine multiply, so the more a medicine is used, the more common resistant germs become.
agreed.evidence: Laboratory tests, including the replica plating of Esther and Joshua Lederberg in 1952, show that a few resistant bacteria are already in a crowd. Hospital records show resistance rising in places where antibiotics are used a lot.

agreed.text: Vaccines teach the body to recognise a germ, without giving the illness.
agreed.evidence: Blood tests show antibodies and memory cells after a vaccine, and vaccinated people get far fewer cases of the illness than unvaccinated people in the same outbreak.

agreed.text: Smallpox has been wiped out by vaccination. Polio has been wiped out in India and most of the world.
agreed.evidence: A world-wide search found no natural case of smallpox after 1977, and the World Health Assembly declared the world free of smallpox in 1980. India reported no wild polio case from 2011, and the region was certified in 2014.

agreed.text: When enough people in a group are vaccinated, people who are not vaccinated are safer too.
agreed.evidence: Measles cases rise in places where fewer than about 95 out of 100 children have both doses, and fall again when vaccination rises.

agreed.text: Oral rehydration solution saves the lives of children with loose motions.
agreed.evidence: Trials and field use since the 1960s show that salt and sugar in clean water replace what the body loses. During a cholera outbreak among refugees in 1971, a team led by Dr Dilip Mahalanabis used it when drips ran short, and far fewer people died.

agreed.text: Side effects of vaccines are usually mild, such as a sore arm or a mild fever for a day. Serious reactions are very rare.
agreed.evidence: Health services track every vaccine given and every report of a reaction, and the risks of the illnesses are much larger than the risks of the vaccines.

challenging.claim: Keep the left-over tablets from last time, because they will work for the next illness.
challenging.who: A common habit in many homes
challenging.for: The packet looks the same and the symptoms seem the same, and tablets cost money.
challenging.against: A cold and a bacterial infection feel alike, but only one needs an antibiotic. A part-used packet is the wrong dose and the wrong length. Medicines also go out of date. Taking antibiotics without need gives tough germs more chances.
challenging.context: This card is about a very common habit with medicines at home.

challenging.claim: A vaccine can give you the illness it is meant to stop.
challenging.for: A vaccine holds a germ or a piece of one. A few vaccines hold a weakened live germ, and in very rare cases that germ can cause a mild form of the illness.
challenging.against: Most vaccines hold killed germs or just one piece, which cannot multiply at all. Even a weakened germ barely multiplies, and the risk of the real illness is far larger than any risk from the vaccine.
challenging.context: This card is about the worry that a vaccine makes you ill with the very germ the vaccine stops.

challenging.claim: It is better to catch the illness than to have a vaccine, because the illness gives stronger protection.
challenging.who: Some parents, and old ideas in many places
challenging.for: For some illnesses, catching the real germ does give long protection, as with chickenpox.
challenging.against: The real illness can cause deafness, blindness, damage to the brain or death. Measles, for example, can harm a child's brain and can also weaken the defences against other germs for a while. A vaccine gives protection without that risk.
challenging.context: This card is about whether it is wiser to catch an illness on purpose.

challenging.claim: A fever is dangerous in itself and must always be brought down quickly.
challenging.for: A very high fever can be frightening and uncomfortable, and in small babies a fever can be a sign of serious illness.
challenging.against: A fever is part of how the body fights an infection, and it is usually not harmful in itself in a healthy child. Doctors often treat the child's comfort, not the number. Scientists are still studying how much a fever helps.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a fever should always be brought down.

challenging.claim: Home remedies like kadha, turmeric milk, tulsi or neem can replace medicine for a serious infection.
challenging.who: Many families, and some traditional healers
challenging.for: Warm drinks, honey for an older child's cough, and rest comfort a child with a cold. Some plants contain substances that do act on microbes, and some medicines, such as quinine, come from plants.
challenging.against: Tests of a plant in a dish are not the same as testing a medicine in a person. For serious infections such as typhoid, tuberculosis or malaria, delay can be dangerous, and tested medicines are needed. Comfort and cure are different jobs.
challenging.context: This card is about the place of traditional remedies next to tested medicines.

challenging.claim: Once you have had a vaccine, you can never catch that illness.
challenging.for: Vaccines work very well, and most vaccinated people never catch the illness.
challenging.against: No vaccine works for every person, and protection can fade, so a few vaccinated people still catch the illness. They usually have a milder illness. That is one reason boosters are given and why herd protection matters.
challenging.context: This card is about how complete the protection of a vaccine is.

challenging.claim: Killing as many germs as possible with strong cleaners and antibacterial products keeps a home healthiest.
challenging.for: Germs cause illness, so fewer germs seem better.
challenging.against: Most microbes are harmless or helpful, and strong cleaners everywhere can help tough germs to take over. Plain soap and water, clean water and clean food break most germ chains. Disinfectants are for particular jobs, such as a toilet or a wound.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a home should be made as germ-free as possible.

big_questions.q: In the rice and dal game, the medicine did not make any germ tougher. It only removed the ordinary ones. So did the medicine cause the tough germs, or did it only uncover them?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the dal grains were before the medicine came, and what the Lederbergs found on the dish that had never met the medicine.

big_questions.q: A vaccine holds no working germ, yet your body remembers a germ that never met this body before. Where is the memory kept?
big_questions.hint: Think about memory cells, and how long a single white blood cell can live. Nobody has a complete answer yet.

big_questions.q: Penicillin bursts bacteria but leaves your cells alone. What does that tell you about the difference between a bacterium and a cell of yours?
big_questions.hint: Think about the cell wall, and about who else has one.

big_questions.q: Your gut holds trillions of bacteria, and an antibiotic kills some of them too. When you take a medicine, who is being treated: you, or a whole crowd that lives in you?
big_questions.hint: Think about the bacteria that help you digest food, and what happens to them.

big_questions.q: A baby too young for a vaccine is protected because other people are vaccinated. Who is protecting whom in a class, and is it fair to ask for it?
big_questions.hint: Think about the child who cannot be vaccinated, and about the child who just does not like the needle.

big_questions.q: Medicines and vaccines are tested on volunteers before they are sold. How do we know a test was fair, and who should decide what counts as safe enough?
big_questions.hint: Think about who is in the test, who pays for it, and who checks the results.

big_questions.q: Some countries can buy a new vaccine early and others must wait for years. Who should get a new vaccine first?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the illness is worst, who makes the vaccine, and what it costs.

big_questions.q: We say we fight germs. Is fight the right word, when most microbes are harmless and a few are only living their own lives?
big_questions.hint: Think about a farmer, a doctor, and a Jain monk, who each see a germ differently.

big_questions.q: For a long time, most doctors believed that illness came from bad air, and many laughed at the idea of tiny living germs. What makes a new idea about something too small to see believable?
big_questions.hint: Think about which evidence is strong enough to change an old idea, and who is willing to look.

story.title: The Round Scar
story.note: The story is made up, but the facts are true. Smallpox killed about three in ten people who caught it. Health workers in India's last years of smallpox found each case and vaccinated the people around it. A vaccine given in the first days after meeting the germ can still protect.
text: Anu was nine, and she lived with her parents and her grandmother in a flat in Kozhikode. Her grandmother was called Muthassi. On Monday, their class teacher, Revathi Miss, gave every child a pink slip.
"The health team is coming on Thursday," said Revathi Miss. "Everyone in Class 4 gets a booster injection. Take the slip home and ask your parents to sign it."

Anu carried the slip home as if it were hot. She did not like needles. She liked even less the idea of a germ being put into her arm on purpose. "Why would anyone put a germ into a healthy girl?" she wondered.

That evening, Muthassi was plaiting Anu's hair on the balcony. Her sari slipped off her shoulder. Anu saw something she had seen a hundred times and never asked about. High on Muthassi's left arm was a round, pale, dented mark, as big as a button.
"Muthassi, what is that?"

"That is my smallpox stamp," said Muthassi. "Have you heard of smallpox?" Anu shook her head. "No child your age has. It was an illness that covered people with sores. About three out of every ten who caught it died. And now it is gone from the whole world."
"Gone? How can an illness be gone?"

"Sit still, and I will tell you. When I was ten, my little brother Gopi woke up hot and shivering, with red spots on his face. In two days the spots were blisters. My father went very quiet, because everyone knew what that meant."

"The next morning, a woman came to our gate on a bicycle, with a cloth bag on the handlebar. She was Thankamma Chechi, the health worker. A neighbour had told her. She did not shout, and she did not run from the house. She sat on our front step with a notebook, and she asked questions."

"Who lives in this house? Who lives next door? Who brings the milk? Who sits beside Gopi at school? She wrote down every name. Then she said, 'By tonight, I need every one of these people in a line.'"

"By evening they were all there. The neighbours, the milkman, Gopi's whole class, and me. Thankamma Chechi dipped a small needle in a drop of liquid and pricked the top of each arm. It stung a little. A week later my arm swelled into a blister, and when it healed, it left this."
"And Gopi?" asked Anu, in a small voice.

"He was ill for many days, and some marks stayed on his face. But he lived. And nobody else in our village got smallpox that year. Nobody. Not the milkman, not the neighbours, not Gopi's classmates. Not even me, and I slept in his room for two weeks to look after him."
Anu frowned. Something did not fit. "But you were right next to him all day, Muthassi. You must have breathed his germs. Why didn't you get ill?"
"What do you think?" said Muthassi.

Anu thought. The drop in the needle must have had something to do with smallpox, or it would not have worked. But Muthassi had only a blister, not smallpox. So the drop must hold something that looks like the germ, but cannot make you really ill.
"The drop was a picture," said Anu slowly. "A picture of the germ, for your body to look at. Your body made antibodies from the picture, and they were ready when Gopi's germs came."
"Yes," said Muthassi. "Mine was made from a mild cousin of the smallpox germ, which cows catch. It is a lesson, not an attack."
"But Muthassi, why did Thankamma Chechi stamp the milkman and the neighbours? They were not Gopi's family."
Muthassi smiled. "Fetch me some rice flour."

Anu came back with a steel plate of rice flour. On the balcony floor, Muthassi made dots in a square, like the start of a kolam. One dot she made red with a pinch of kumkum. "That is Gopi's house. If a germ goes from house to house, which dots will the germ reach first?"
Anu pointed to the dots that touched the red one. "Those. And then the ones touching those."
"Now, if every one of those dots around the red one has a stamp?"
Anu rubbed white flour over the dots around the red one. Then she saw it. The germ had nowhere to go. A ring of protected people around the ill one, and the germ was stuck.
"So the stamp was not only for you," she said. "It was for the milkman and the neighbours, and for everyone in the next village too."
"For all of them," said Muthassi. "That is why Thankamma Chechi cycled from house to house. Every stamp was a gap in the road the germ wanted to travel."

On Thursday, Anu stood in the line outside the school hall. The health worker was a young woman with a steady hand. "It will sting for a moment," she said. Anu looked at the small raised dot on her own arm, from a vaccine she had as a baby. She took a breath, counted to three, and looked away. It stung. Then it was done.
That evening she showed Muthassi the plaster. Then she took the rice flour and drew the dots again, on the doorstep, with a ring of white around one red dot.
Muthassi touched her round scar and smiled. "Our whole village was in that picture," she said. "And now you are in it too."
story.epiphany: A vaccine shows the body a safe picture of a germ, so the body is ready when the real germ arrives. When the people around an ill person are protected, the germ has nowhere to go, and the chain stops.
ask: Why did Thankamma Chechi vaccinate the milkman and the neighbours, and not only Gopi's family?
How could Muthassi sleep in Gopi's room for two weeks and stay well?
What did the ring of white flour show Anu about how a germ spreads?
Anu was afraid of the needle at the start. What changed her mind, and was it a fear or a fact that changed?

roots.context: We have watched a medicine leave a few tough germs behind, and a vaccine teach a body before the germ arrives. Now we ask what these tell us about the fight we call health, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the rice and dal game, the medicine did not make any germ tougher. It removed the ordinary ones, and the few tough ones carried on. So the germs of tomorrow are the survivors of what we do today. We are part of the fight, not outside it.
deep_truth.habit: We picture illness as a war between us and a fixed enemy called germs. But germs are never all the same, and the ones that survive our medicines become the next crowd.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Rice and Dal game, the plate with the medicine ended with mostly tough germs, and the plate with no medicine kept its ordinary crowd. Esther Lederberg's velvet stamp showed that real resistant bacteria were already on a dish that had never met the medicine.

three.who_am_i: You are a body that remembers. Your defenders keep a record of the germs you have met, and a vaccine can add to that record without making you ill.
three.what_is_life: A crowd of bacteria is never all the same. A few differ by chance, and when the world changes, those few carry on. Life goes on because it is varied.
three.what_is_this_world: People, medicines and germs shape each other. Our medicines decide which germs live, and the germs that live decide which medicines we must make next.

roots.thread: In the game, a crowd that looked all the same held a few that were different. When the medicine came, those few became the future. A world that holds many kinds can survive a change that would end a world of one kind. Your own defenders work this way too: your body makes millions of kinds of antibody before any germ arrives, and the germ finds the one that fits. Nobody plans the variety. It is how life keeps going when conditions change.

teachings.teaching: Act on things before they appear. Put things in order before there is confusion. A tree that fills your arms grew from a tiny shoot.
teachings.link: A vaccine acts before the germ arrives. A small step early prevents a large trouble later.

teachings.source: Louis Pasteur, opening lecture at the University of Lille, 7 December 1854
teachings.teaching: In the fields of observation, chance favours only the prepared mind.
teachings.link: Fleming saw a clear ring round a mould because he was ready to notice the ring. A body that has met a vaccine is prepared in the same way, and the real germ finds defenders ready.

teachings.teaching: Find out the illness, find out its cause, find out the cure, and then treat with care.
teachings.link: A doctor chooses a medicine by the cause. A cold and a bacterial throat infection feel alike, but they have different causes and need different help.

science.text: Resistant bacteria are already present in a crowd before a medicine arrives. The medicine selects them, and they multiply. This is natural selection.
How the body keeps a memory of a germ for decades, and how long that memory lasts for each germ, is still being studied.

other_view.view: Saying that germs and medicines 'shape each other' is a picture. A bacterium copies her genes with small mistakes, and a medicine sorts the copies. That is all the evidence needs. Calling it a fight, or a conversation, adds a story that the evidence does not require.

practice.title: Feel your pulse: the blood that carries your defenders
practice.say: Sit still. Press two fingers on the inside of your wrist, below the thumb, until you feel your pulse. Each beat pushes blood past defenders that are patrolling right now. Some of them hold the memory of germs you met as a baby. Breathe in slowly and out slowly. Count ten beats. Then rest your hand in your lap.
practice.kid: Sit still. Find your pulse on your wrist. Your blood carries your defenders. Breathe slowly. Count ten beats.

ask: If a medicine decides which germs carry on, who is shaping whom? Are we shaping the germs, or are the germs shaping the medicines we make?
Your defenders remember germs you met when you were too young to remember anything yourself. Who is the you that remembers?
Esther Lederberg's name is often left out of the story of her own discovery. How can we know who did a piece of science, and who should get the credit?
roots.art: Two plates side by side: one with a few green dal grains among many white rice grains, and the same plate after a medicine with only green grains left, and a child's pulse drawn as a small wave between them.

games.title: Medicine or Not? Choose the best response
games.context: This is a sorting card game. Each card describes an illness or a situation. You decide which response fits best: a germ-killing medicine chosen by a doctor, rest and drinks, ORS, a vaccine, or a doctor at once.

printables.title: 5 response cards
items: GERM-KILLING MEDICINE: a doctor has found the cause and chooses a medicine that works on that germ.
REST AND DRINKS: the body's defenders do the work. Warm drinks and rest help.
ORS: the body is losing water and salts, and ORS puts them back.
VACCINE: it prevents the illness before the germ comes.
DOCTOR AT ONCE: a danger sign, or a serious illness that needs a test.

printables.title: 18 situation cards (the best response is on the back)

items.f: Divya has a runny nose and a mild cough for two days. She feels well enough to play.
items.b: REST AND DRINKS. A cold is caused by a virus, so an antibiotic would do nothing.

items.f: Farhan has had loose motions three times today and feels thirsty. He can still drink.
items.b: ORS. His body is losing water and salts. Tell a doctor if it goes on or if he cannot drink.

items.f: A doctor tests Tara's sore throat and finds the bacteria that cause the sore throat.
items.b: GERM-KILLING MEDICINE. The doctor found bacteria, so an antibiotic chosen by the doctor can work.

items.f: A baby is born. She is a few days old.
items.b: VACCINE. In India a newborn is given the first vaccines soon after birth, for tuberculosis, polio and hepatitis B.

items.f: Arjun has body ache, a high fever and a cough. The doctor says it is flu and he is otherwise healthy.
items.b: REST AND DRINKS. Flu is caused by a virus, so an antibiotic does not help. A doctor may give an antiviral to people at high risk.

items.f: A stray dog bites Lakshmi on the leg near the bus stop in Chennai.
items.b: DOCTOR AT ONCE. Wash the bite with soap and running water for several minutes, then go to a doctor for the rabies vaccine the same day.

items.f: Meenakshi's little brother is nine months old.
items.b: VACCINE. In India, the measles and rubella vaccine is given to babies at about this age.

items.f: Rahul has had a cough for three weeks and he is losing weight.
items.b: DOCTOR AT ONCE. A cough that lasts more than two weeks needs a test, for example for tuberculosis.

items.f: Priya has chickenpox spots and a mild fever. She is playing quietly.
items.b: REST AND DRINKS. Chickenpox is caused by a virus. A doctor can advise, and she stays home so she does not pass it on.

items.f: Kavya has a cold. Her friend says her left-over tablets from last month would help.
items.b: REST AND DRINKS. Left-over tablets are not for a new illness. A doctor must say which medicine is right.

items.f: A child has loose motions, cannot keep any drink down and is very sleepy.
items.b: DOCTOR AT ONCE. Not being able to drink and being very sleepy are danger signs.

items.f: Ayesha has a deep cut from a rusty nail, and she has not had a tetanus booster for years.
items.b: DOCTOR AT ONCE. Tetanus bacteria live in soil and can get into deep cuts. A doctor decides about cleaning and a booster.

items.f: A doctor finds that Nandini's itchy round rash is ringworm.
items.b: GERM-KILLING MEDICINE. Ringworm is caused by a fungus, so the doctor gives an antifungal cream, not an antibiotic.

items.f: Gowri is ten years old and the school health team is coming with the booster against tetanus and diphtheria.
items.b: VACCINE. A booster tops up the memory cells that fade over the years.

items.f: A baby of five months has a fever of 39 degrees and is crying without stopping.
items.b: DOCTOR AT ONCE. In a small baby, a high fever can be a sign of serious illness.

items.f: Sneha has a blocked nose and a scratchy throat. Her teacher says, give her an antibiotic and she will be fine by morning.
items.b: REST AND DRINKS. A scratchy throat with a cold is usually a virus. If it gets worse or lasts, a doctor can test for bacteria.

items.f: Bhavna has watery loose motions after a wedding feast. She has also been vomiting, but she can still sip.
items.b: ORS. Small, frequent sips of ORS keep her from drying out. If she cannot keep it down, she needs a doctor.

items.f: A doctor finds that Thatha's chest infection is caused by bacteria that are resistant to the usual antibiotic.
items.b: GERM-KILLING MEDICINE. The doctor chooses a different medicine after testing, which is why tests matter.

rules: Lay the five response cards in a row on the table. Shuffle the situation cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back. With three or four players, pass the reader's job to the left after each card.

Turn the card over and read the back. A player scores 1 point for the best response and 1 more point for a reason that names the cause, such as a virus, bacteria, lost water or a danger sign.
Playing alone? Read the card to yourself, choose and say your reason aloud, and then turn the card over.
This game teaches general ideas. It is not advice for your own family. For a real illness, ask a doctor or a health worker.

rules: One player is the Germ keeper and the other is the Health worker. Playing alone? Play both parts, and be fair to both. With three or four players, make two teams: a Germ team, who put the red token and spread the illness, and a Health team, who place the vaccine tokens.

Round 1, nobody vaccinated: the Germ keeper puts the red token on house C3. At the end of each week, the illness spreads to every neighbour of an ill house. Put a red mark on each newly ill house. Play four weeks and count all the ill houses, including C3.

Round 2, a ring at once: start again with house C3 ill. Before each week's spread, the Health worker puts 3 vaccine tokens on houses that are not ill. A vaccinated house can never become ill. Play four weeks and count.

Round 3, a ring one week late: start again with house C3 ill. The Health worker puts no tokens in week 1, because nobody has noticed yet. From week 2, the Health worker puts 3 tokens before each spread. Play four weeks and count.

Round 4, vaccinated first: clear the board. Shuffle the 36 house slips and deal one to each house. Put a vaccine token on every house whose slip says VACCINATED. The Germ keeper picks any NOT YET house and puts the red token there. Play four weeks with no new tokens and count the ill houses.
Round 5, only a third vaccinated: deal again. Turn 12 of the VACCINATED slips so that they count as NOT YET. Play as in Round 4 and count.
Write each count on the score sheet. Compare the five numbers. The Health worker wins a round by keeping the count low.

flow.do: 1. Draw the 6 by 6 board on a large sheet of paper. 2. Cut out the 36 house slips and the tokens. 3. Read the rules together.
flow.say: This village has 36 houses. An illness spreads from an ill house to its neighbours every week. Our job is to find out how to stop it.
flow.kid: Draw a board of 36 squares. Cut out the slips and tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ring the Germ. You build the village and learn how the illness spreads.

flow.do: Play Round 1. Put the red token on C3. Spread the illness for four weeks and count the ill houses.
flow.say: Nobody is vaccinated. Spread the illness week by week. How many houses are ill after four weeks?
flow.kid: Play Round 1. Spread the illness. Count the ill houses.
flow.parent: A correct count after four weeks is 31 houses. After week 1 there are 5, after week 2 there are 13, and after week 3 there are 23. If your child gets a different number, count the spread again, one week at a time.

check.q: In Round 1 the illness spread to 31 of the 36 houses in four weeks. Why did it spread so fast?
options: Every newly ill house passed it on to its neighbours the next week
The germ was getting stronger each week
The Health worker was slow
check.why: Each new case becomes a new source, so the number grows faster each week. The germ did not change. The chain simply had no broken links.

flow.do: Play Round 2 and then Round 3. Count the ill houses each time.
flow.say: Now the Health worker places 3 vaccine tokens before every spread. Where will you put them? Then try again, one week late.
flow.kid: Play Round 2 and Round 3. Place 3 tokens each week. Count the ill houses.
flow.parent: A good ring in Round 2 can stop the illness at 2 to 4 ill houses. Place tokens on the neighbours of the ill houses first. In Round 3 the same careful play usually ends with about 17 to 23 ill houses.

ask.q: What difference did one week make?
good: The illness had already reached more houses before the ring began, so there were many more neighbours to protect.
Acting early keeps the number of ill houses small.

flow.do: Play Round 4 and Round 5. Count the ill houses each time. Write down all five counts.
flow.say: Now people are vaccinated before the illness arrives. First two thirds of the village, then only a third. Which village is safer?
flow.kid: Deal the slips. Place the vaccine tokens. Play Round 4 and Round 5.
flow.parent: With two thirds vaccinated, the illness usually stays at 1 to 6 houses. With a third, it often reaches 5 to 17. Chance changes the results, so playing each round twice gives a fairer picture. Shuffle and deal the slips again each time. These numbers are typical, not promises, and a clever Germ keeper can choose a worse starting house.

check.q: In Rounds 4 and 5 nobody could add new tokens. Why was the village with more vaccinated houses safer?
options: The illness kept meeting vaccinated houses and had fewer paths to follow
The vaccine cured the ill houses
The illness got tired
check.why: A vaccinated house is a broken link. With many broken links the illness cannot find a path across the village. A vaccine does not cure someone already ill. It protects people who are not yet ill.

flow.do: Compare the five counts on the score sheet. Talk about which helped most, and which one a village can do before an illness arrives.
flow.say: Which round gave the smallest count? Which one can a village do before any illness arrives? What would that mean for a baby who cannot be vaccinated?
flow.kid: Look at your five counts. Which was smallest? Which can a village do before the illness?
flow.think: Why is the best protection the one done before anyone is ill?

setup.caption: 1. Draw the board and put the red token on house C3.

setup.art: The same grid with vaccine tokens placed on the four squares around the ill house, and the illness arrows stopped.
setup.caption: 2. Place vaccine tokens around the ill house to make a ring.

setup.art: A grid with most squares covered by vaccine tokens and the red token alone in the middle of a few uncovered squares.
setup.caption: 3. Vaccinate most of the village first, then see how far the illness goes.

experiments.title: The Yeast Test: which kitchen things really slow down a living microbe?
experiments.question: Salt, vinegar, garlic and turmeric are used in pickles and home remedies, and people say they stop microbes. If we add each one to a glass of yeast, a living microbe, which one slows her bubbles the most?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which thing will slow the yeast the most? Which will slow her the least? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every glass gets the same warm water, the same sugar and the same yeast, stirred for the same time. Only the thing we add changes. One glass gets nothing added, so we can see how much foam is normal. All the glasses stand side by side in the same place, and we measure them at the same moment.
results_table: My guess: more foam or less foam than the Plain glass?

materials.item: 5 clear glasses of the same size, each holding at least 250 millilitres. Tall, narrow tumblers show the foam best.
1 sachet of dry baking yeast, about 7 grams. Each glass uses half a level teaspoon.
5 level teaspoons of sugar
a small steel katori or cup, to measure the same amount of warm water for every glass, about 100 millilitres
a jug of warm water, only hand-warm like a baby's bath, about 600 millilitres
2 level teaspoons of salt, 4 teaspoons of white vinegar, 1 clove of garlic and 2 level teaspoons of turmeric powder
a teaspoon, and a spoon for stirring that you wash between glasses
a chopping board and a knife, for a grown-up to crush the garlic
a ruler with millimetres, sticky tape and a marker pen for labels
a timer or a phone clock

experiments.safety: Use warm water only, never hot, because very hot water can scald. A grown-up crushes the garlic with a knife. Do not taste or drink any glass. Keep the glasses away from babies and pets. Vinegar and garlic can sting the eyes, so do not rub them, and rinse with clean water if a drop splashes in. If anyone at home is allergic to any of these foods, leave that glass out and do not let that person handle it. Wash hands after handling garlic. At the end, pour everything down the sink and wash the glasses with soap.

schedule.what: Label five glasses. Add warm water, sugar and yeast. Add one test thing to each. Wait 20 minutes, then measure the foam in each glass.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for each glass, as tall as its foam, starting with the Plain glass. If you measured at 10 minutes too, mark that number on each bar with a line.
experiments.context: In this experiment you add salt, vinegar, garlic and turmeric to separate glasses of yeast, and measure which one holds back the foam. Yeast is a living microbe, so the test shows how a germ-killer works without any risk of illness.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: foam height after 20 minutes

setup.art: Five clear glasses in a row on a tray, labelled Plain, Salt, Vinegar, Garlic and Turmeric, each with the same level of warm water.
setup.caption: 1. Label five glasses. Pour the same warm water into each.

setup.art: A hand adding half a teaspoon of dry yeast and a teaspoon of sugar to a glass of water, with a spoon beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Add one teaspoon of sugar and half a teaspoon of yeast. Stir for 10 seconds.

setup.art: Four small bowls of salt, vinegar, crushed garlic and turmeric beside the first four glasses, and nothing next to the Plain glass.
setup.caption: 3. Add a different test thing to each glass. The Plain glass gets nothing.

setup.art: A ruler held against a glass with a layer of foam on top, measuring the height of the foam in millimetres.
setup.caption: 4. After 20 minutes, measure the foam in each glass.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the five glasses, the yeast, the sugar and the four test things. 2. Say that yeast is a tiny living fungus who makes bubbles when she eats sugar. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason. 4. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Yeast is a tiny living fungus. When she eats sugar, she makes bubbles of gas and a layer of foam. Salt, vinegar, garlic and turmeric are used in pickles and home remedies, and people say they stop microbes. Which will stop the yeast most? Which will stop her least? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Yeast is a tiny living fungus. She eats sugar and makes foam. Which kitchen thing will stop her most? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that thing will stop the yeast?
good: Salt dries things out, so pickles keep.
Vinegar is sour, and sour things do not spoil easily.
Garlic and turmeric are used as medicine.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. A guess with a reason is a good start. Yeast does not make people ill. She is a safe stand-in for a microbe, so the test works like a germ-killer test without any danger. One child with a parent: the child does the pouring, stirring and measuring while the parent crushes the garlic and keeps the clock. Two to four children: each child owns one glass and does its sugar, yeast and test thing, and measures its own foam; the Plain glass is shared and measured by the youngest. Everyone stirs for the same 10 seconds, counted aloud.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Yeast Test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Stick a strip of tape on each glass and write Plain, Salt, Vinegar, Garlic and Turmeric. 2. Pour one katori of warm water into every glass. 3. Fill the katori to the same line each time.
flow.say: Warm water, not hot. Hot water would kill the yeast. Use the same katori, filled to the same line, for every glass.
flow.kid: Label the five glasses. Pour the same warm water into each one.

check.q: Why do all five glasses get the same warm water, the same sugar and the same yeast?
options: So that only the thing we add is different
So the glasses look neat
Because yeast needs five spoons
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one glass had more sugar, we would not know whether the foam came from the sugar or from the thing we added. Neat glasses look nice, but that is not why they match.

flow.context: In this step you set out the glasses and measure the same warm water into each.

flow.do: 1. Put 1 level teaspoon of sugar into every glass. 2. Add half a level teaspoon of yeast to every glass. 3. Stir each glass for 10 seconds with a clean spoon. 4. Add 2 teaspoons of salt to the Salt glass. 5. Add 4 teaspoons of vinegar to the Vinegar glass. 6. Add the crushed garlic to the Garlic glass. 7. Add 2 teaspoons of turmeric to the Turmeric glass. 8. Stir each glass again for 10 seconds. 9. Write down the start time.
flow.say: The Plain glass gets nothing extra. That is our comparison. Stir each glass for the same time. Now write the time, and start the clock.
flow.kid: Add sugar and yeast to every glass. Add the test things. Write the start time.
flow.parent: A grown-up crushes one garlic clove on the board with the flat of the knife until it is a paste, and puts all of it into the Garlic glass. Wash the spoon between glasses. The Salt glass may not dissolve fully, and that is fine.
flow.context: In this step you add the yeast, the sugar and one test thing to each glass, and start the clock.

flow.do: 1. Look at the glasses every 5 minutes. 2. Draw what you see in each. 3. At 10 minutes, quickly measure the foam in each glass and write it beside the table. 4. Wait until 20 minutes have passed since you stirred.
flow.say: Look at the glasses every five minutes. Which glass starts to foam first? Which stays flat? Draw what you see.
flow.kid: Look at the glasses every five minutes. Draw what you see.

ask.q: What do you think is making the bubbles and foam?
good: The yeast is making gas.
The yeast is eating the sugar and breathing out bubbles.

flow.parent: Yeast is slow in the first minutes. Bubbles usually start to appear by 5 to 10 minutes in the Plain glass. If nothing at all has happened in the Plain glass after 15 minutes, the water was probably too cold or too hot, or the yeast is old. Start again with fresh yeast and hand-warm water. If the Plain glass has only a thin foam of under 5 millimetres at 20 minutes, give every glass 10 more minutes and measure all of them again, so they stay fair. In hot weather the foam comes faster, so measure a little earlier. In a cold room, stand the glasses together in a tray of hand-warm water. Yeast sachets from different shops behave a little differently, so only compare glasses made with the same sachet.
flow.context: In this step you wait and watch the glasses for 20 minutes.

flow.do: 1. After 20 minutes, hold the ruler beside each glass. 2. Measure the height of the foam, from the water up to the top of the foam, in millimetres. 3. Write the number in the table. 4. Wave the air above each glass towards your nose and write what you smell.
flow.say: Measure from the water up to the top of the foam. If there is no foam, write zero. Then wave the air gently towards your nose.
flow.kid: Measure the foam in each glass. Write the number. Wave the smell to your nose.
flow.parent: Typical pattern, not a promise: a thick foam on the Plain glass and a similar one on the Turmeric glass, much less on the Salt glass, and less than Plain on the Vinegar and Garlic glasses. Your own result is the real one. If the glasses behave differently, write it down. Different yeast, water and room temperature can change the numbers.
flow.context: In this step you measure the foam in every glass and write down the results.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: What do you think happened? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened that way?
flow.kid: Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

check.q: The Salt glass had much less foam than the Plain glass. What does this show?
options: Strong salt slowed or stopped the yeast
Salt makes yeast eat faster
Salt made the water colder
check.why: The water, the sugar and the yeast were the same in both glasses. Only the salt was different, so the salt held back the yeast. Strong salt pulls water out of microbes, which is why salted foods keep. It would also harm our own cells, so we do not drink salt water to treat an infection.

ask.q: What I think, what I saw, and why?
good: What I think: strong salt and vinegar slow microbes. What I saw: less foam in those glasses. Why: they make it hard for yeast to live.

flow.context: In this step you say what you think, what you saw, and why.

flow.do: 1. Pour all the glasses down the sink. 2. Wash the glasses and spoons with soap. 3. Wash your hands with soap, because of the garlic. 4. Ask the question below.
flow.say: A real germ-killer must hurt the germ and not hurt you. Which of our glasses held back the yeast? Would that thing be safe to put into a body?
flow.kid: Pour the glasses out. Wash everything with soap. Wash your hands.
flow.think: A medicine must hurt the germ and not you. Why can't we drink strong salt water or vinegar to cure an infection?
flow.context: In this step you clean up and think about what a safe germ-killer must do.

experiments.title: Rice and Dal: what is left after the medicine?
experiments.question: A medicine kills nearly all the ordinary germs in a body, but a few tough germs survive it. What does the crowd of germs look like after three days with the medicine, and after three days without it?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After three days, how many of the 40 germs will be tough ones with the medicine, and how many without? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both plates start the same, with 38 ordinary germs and 2 tough germs. Both follow the same rules each night. Only one thing is different. Plate A gets the medicine every day, and Plate B never does. When the germs are picked for the crowding step, you pick without looking, so that nothing is chosen on purpose. If you can, play the game twice, because chance changes the numbers a little.

materials.item: about 300 grains of white rice (a small katori full), as the ordinary germs
30 whole green moong grains, or any dal that looks clearly different from the rice, as the tough germs. If you have only one kind of dal, use brown and white rice.
2 large plates, one marked A and one marked B, as the two bodies
a small bowl for mixing, and a spoon for picking
paper and a pencil, to write the table. Counting in fives and tens makes it quicker.

experiments.safety: Keep rice and dal away from babies and small children, who may put grains in their mouth or nose. Do not eat the grains afterwards if they have been handled a lot. Wash your hands when you finish.

schedule.what: Set up Plate A and Plate B. Play three days on each plate. Write the table. Compare the plates.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the two plates at the end of Day 3, with the rice and dal grains drawn in two colours.
experiments.context: In this experiment you use rice and dal as pretend germs, and a rule for what a medicine does, to find out which germs are left after three days with and without the medicine.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results at the end of each day

setup.art: Two large plates marked A and B, each holding a heap of 38 white rice grains and 2 green moong grains.
setup.caption: 1. Put 38 rice grains and 2 dal grains on each plate.

setup.art: A hand adding the same number of rice grains to a plate of rice, so the heap doubles, while dal grains are doubled beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Each night, every germ splits in two. Add as many grains of each kind as there are on the plate.

setup.art: All the grains mixed in a bowl and a child looking away while she picks 40 grains back on to the plate.
setup.caption: 3. If there are more than 40, mix and pick 40 without looking.

setup.art: Plate A with a pile of rice grains in groups of ten, and one grain from each group kept while the rest are swept away.
setup.caption: 4. On Plate A only, the medicine takes all but one ordinary germ from each pile of ten.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the rice, the dal and the two plates. 2. Say that rice grains are ordinary germs and dal grains are tough germs. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason. 4. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.say: These grains are pretend germs. Rice is the ordinary germ. Dal is a germ who happens to be tough against a medicine. Plate A will get the medicine every day. Plate B will not. After three days, how many tough germs will each plate have? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Rice is the ordinary germ. Dal is the tough germ. Guess how many tough germs each plate will have. Why?

ask.q: What makes you think the plate with medicine will have more tough germs?
good: The medicine kills the ordinary ones, so only the tough ones are left.
The medicine makes the tough ones stronger.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Some children think the medicine makes germs tougher. Write that down and let the game answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Rice and Dal. You guess before you play.

flow.do: 1. Count 38 rice grains on to Plate A. 2. Add 2 dal grains. 3. Do the same on Plate B. 4. Write the start numbers in the table.
