flow.say: Each plate is a body with 40 germs. Most are ordinary. Two are tough, and they were already a little different before any medicine arrived. Each body has food for only 40 germs.
flow.kid: Put 38 rice grains and 2 dal grains on each plate.
flow.context: In this step you set up the two bodies, each with 40 germs.
flow.parent: One child with a parent: the child runs both plates, and the parent mixes, hides the picking and checks the counts. Two to four children: one child is Plate A's keeper, one is Plate B's keeper, one mixes and picks without looking, and one writes the table. Swap roles on the next game. Each plate needs its own space, so use two plates and a shared supply bowl. Count out the rice in fives to go quickly.

flow.do: Play Day 1 on Plate B, with no medicine. 1. Night: count the rice grains on the plate and add the same number from the supply. 2. Do the same with the dal grains. 3. Crowding: put all the grains in the bowl and mix. 4. Look away and pick 40 grains, one at a time, back on to the plate. 5. Count the rice and the dal on the plate and write the numbers.
flow.say: At night every germ splits in two, so each kind doubles. But the body has food for only 40 germs, so the rest die. We pick the 40 without looking, so the picking is fair.
flow.kid: Add the same number of grains to each kind. Mix. Pick 40 without looking. Count.
flow.parent: On Plate B there are 76 rice and 4 dal after the night, which makes 80 grains. You pick 40 of the 80. The dal share usually stays small, around 2 out of 40. Chance changes it, so 1 or 3 is normal. Slow children can count rice in fives. If you run short of time, stop after Day 2 and finish Day 3 later; leave the plates as they are and write the table first.
flow.context: In this step you play the first day on Plate B, the plate with no medicine.

flow.do: Play Day 1 on Plate A, with the medicine. 1. Night: double each kind. 2. Crowding: if there are more than 40 grains, mix and pick 40 without looking. 3. Medicine: put the rice grains into piles of ten. Keep one grain from each pile and take away all the rest, including any left-over rice. 4. The medicine does not touch the dal. 5. Count the rice and the dal and write the numbers.
flow.say: The medicine kills nearly all the ordinary germs. In each pile of ten, only one survives. But the medicine does not kill the tough germs, so every dal grain stays.
flow.kid: Double each kind. Pick 40. Make piles of ten rice grains. Keep one from each pile.
flow.parent: After the medicine, Plate A usually holds about 3 rice grains and about 2 dal grains, in a plate that had 40 grains this morning. Many children are surprised how empty the plate looks. About one game in seventeen, chance throws both dal grains out in the crowding step on Day 1, and Plate A is then left empty. That is a real result, because with no tough germ the medicine wins. Write it down and play again.
flow.context: In this step you play the first day on Plate A, the plate that gets the medicine.

flow.do: Play Day 2 and Day 3 on both plates, with the same rules. Write the table after each day. Remember, only Plate A gets the medicine.
flow.say: Same rules each day. Double each kind. Pick 40 only if there are more than 40. Plate A gets the medicine again. Write the numbers each day.
flow.kid: Play Day 2 and Day 3 on both plates. Write the numbers each day.

check.q: On Plate A, by Day 2 there are almost no rice grains left. Why do the dal grains keep growing in number?
options: Each night the surviving tough germs split in two, and the medicine does not remove them
The medicine feeds the dal grains
Dal grains are heavier than rice
check.why: The medicine removes the ordinary germs, but the tough germs survive. Each night every surviving tough germ splits in two, so their number doubles. The medicine did not feed them. It only took away the others, which left them room and food.

flow.parent: On Plate A, a typical run is 3 rice and 2 dal after Day 1, then 0 rice and 4 dal after Day 2, then 0 rice and 8 dal after Day 3. On Plate B, a typical run keeps about 38 rice and 2 dal each day, though chance may give 1, 3 or 4 dal. About one game in four, the dal on Plate B disappear by chance, because only a few grains can be thrown out by luck. That is a real result. Write it down and play again.
flow.context: In this step you play Day 2 and Day 3 on both plates.

flow.do: 1. Count the grains on both plates. 2. Look at the table together. 3. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: What do you think happened? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened that way? Which plate holds more tough germs, and which has more room for them?
flow.kid: Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: What I think, what I saw, and why?
good: What I think: the medicine does not make germs tough, it removes the ordinary ones. What I saw: Plate A ended with mostly dal, and Plate B stayed mostly rice. Why: with the ordinary germs gone, the tough ones had all the room and food.

ask.q: On Plate B, why did the dal stay so few?
good: The rice used up the food and room, so the dal could not take over.
Every night half of the grains were picked away, rice and dal alike.

flow.context: In this step you say what you think, what you saw, and why.

flow.do: Read the fact aloud. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Real bacteria work like this. A crowd of billions has a few that are tough before any medicine arrives. In 1952, Esther Lederberg showed this with a velvet stamp. The medicine does not teach them. It only decides which ones carry on. Why might a doctor avoid giving an antibiotic when it is not needed?
flow.kid: Real germs work like this. The medicine only chooses which ones carry on.

check.q: A family takes an antibiotic for a cold, which is caused by a virus. Why is this a bad idea?
options: It cannot help the cold, and it gives tough bacteria in the body a chance to take over
It makes the cold virus tougher
It makes the person tougher against all germs
check.why: An antibiotic does nothing to a virus, so the antibiotic cannot help a cold. But the antibiotic still removes ordinary bacteria in the body and leaves room for tough ones. A virus does not become tougher, because the antibiotic never touched them.

flow.think: In the game, who made the tough germs: the medicine, or chance? Where were the dal grains before the medicine began?
flow.context: In this step you connect the game to real bacteria.

activities.title: The Medicine Box Detective

materials.item: the medicine box or shelf at home. If there is no box, a few empty strips and bottles from a neighbour or a chemist, with the grown-up's permission.
a table, paper and a pencil, to write the table
a grown-up, who takes out and handles every medicine

activities.safety: A grown-up takes out the medicines and holds them. A child reads the labels but does not open any bottle or tablet strip, and never tastes anything. Keep medicines out of reach of small children. Put expired medicines aside for a grown-up to return to a chemist or health centre, and never flush them or throw them in a drain.

schedule.what: Lay out the medicines. Read each label. Sort them into what they do. Find any that have expired.

activities.record: A table with columns: name, what it is for, does it kill a germ or ease a sign, and the expiry date.
activities.context: In this activity you read the labels in your own medicine box, and sort the medicines by what they actually do.

setup.art: A family medicine box open on a table with strips, bottles and tubes laid out in rows and a child reading a label.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up lays out the medicines. You read the labels.

setup.art: Four small piles of medicines: one for germs, one for easing signs, one for the skin, and one with expired dates set aside.
setup.caption: 2. Sort them into piles, and put expired ones aside.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up brings the medicine box to the table and lays out everything. 2. Ask your child to guess how many of the medicines kill germs. 3. Write the guess.
flow.say: Let's look at what is in our medicine box. How many of these do you think kill germs? How many only ease a sign, like pain or fever? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A grown-up lays out the medicines. Guess how many kill germs. Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Medicine Box Detective. You guess before you read.

flow.do: 1. Read the front of each packet: the name, what it is for, and the expiry date. 2. Write each in the table. 3. Mark whether it kills a germ, eases a sign, or is for the skin.
flow.say: Read the name and what it is for. The line that says what it contains tells you more than the brand name. Does the medicine kill a germ, or only ease a sign like pain, fever or an itch?
flow.kid: Read each label. Write the name and what it is for. Do not open anything.
flow.parent: Most home boxes hold medicines that ease signs, such as fever and pain medicine, plus ORS, creams and an antiseptic. Antibiotics should not be in a home box, because they are given for a particular illness. If there are some left over, ask a doctor or pharmacist what to do with them. One child with a parent: the child reads and writes, the parent holds each packet. Two to four children: each child takes one group of medicines and fills in their own rows; then they swap and check each other. Also look for two packets that share the same active ingredient name, which is a good lesson in not giving two medicines for the same thing.

check.q: A tube says it is a cream for itchy skin. Does it kill the germ that causes a cold?
options: No, it eases a sign on the skin
Yes, all medicines kill germs
Yes, because it is a cream
check.why: A cream for itching works on the skin. A cold is caused by a virus in the nose and throat, and no cream reaches that. Many home medicines ease signs. Only a few kill germs.

flow.context: In this step you read the labels and fill in the table.

flow.do: 1. Find any medicine whose expiry date has passed. 2. Put those in a separate bag for the grown-up to return to a chemist. 3. Check that the box is out of reach of small children.
flow.say: A medicine can lose strength after its date, and some can become harmful. Which of ours have run out of date? Is our box somewhere a little child cannot reach?
flow.kid: Find any medicine past its date. A grown-up puts those in a bag.
flow.context: In this step you look for expired medicines and check the box is safe.

flow.do: Count the medicines in each group and talk about the result.
flow.say: How many kill a germ? How many only ease a sign? Was your guess close? Why do you think a doctor chooses very carefully when to use a germ-killing medicine?
flow.kid: Count the piles. Was your guess close?

ask.q: Which medicines in the box do something about the germ?
good: Perhaps only the antiseptic for the skin.
Few or none. Most medicines at home ease signs.

flow.context: In this step you count the piles and compare them with your guess.

activities.title: Memory Cards: how a vaccine saves time

materials.item: 33 small squares of paper, about 5 centimetres wide. 30 are antibody cards and 3 are germ cards.
a pen
a phone or clock with a stopwatch
a helper, who holds the germ cards and the stopwatch
a table or a clear patch of floor

schedule.what: Make 30 antibody cards and 3 germ cards. Time four searches. Compare the times.

activities.record: A table with the four times in seconds: first meeting, second meeting, no vaccine, after a vaccine. Then draw a bar for each time.
activities.context: In this activity you play the part of the body's defenders and time how long it takes to find the right antibody. You find out how much time a vaccine saves.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: seconds to find the right antibody

setup.art: Thirty small paper cards spread face up on a table, each with a different three-letter code written on it.
setup.caption: 1. Write a different code on each of 30 cards and spread them on the table.

setup.art: A helper holding up a germ card with a code, while a child searches the spread cards and a stopwatch runs.
setup.caption: 2. A germ arrives. Search for the matching antibody card and time it.

setup.art: A small pile of matching cards kept to the side, labelled 'memory', and a child reaching for it first.
setup.caption: 3. Keep each match you find in a memory pile, and look there first next time.

flow.do: 1. Explain the game. 2. Ask your child to guess how many times faster the search is after a vaccine. 3. Write the guess.
flow.say: Your body has defenders that fit one germ each. You are the defenders now. A germ card will arrive, and you must find the matching antibody card. How much faster will you be if a vaccine showed you the germ first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You are the body's defenders. A germ card arrives. Find the matching antibody. Guess how fast.
flow.context: This is the first step of Memory Cards. You guess before you play.

flow.do: 1. Write a different three-letter code on each of 30 cards. Use codes like KRT, PAM or LOB, and no two the same. 2. The helper secretly chooses three codes and writes each on a germ card. 3. Spread the 30 antibody cards face up on the table.
flow.say: Each antibody card has its own code. Each germ card matches exactly one of them. The helper picks three germs in secret, so you will not know which cards to look for.
flow.kid: Write 30 different codes on 30 cards. The helper writes three germ cards.
flow.parent: Help your child write the codes quickly. The three germ cards must each match one antibody card exactly, and the helper must keep them hidden from the searcher. Name the germ cards 1, 2 and 3. Use codes that look alike in a few cases, such as KRT and KRL, so the search takes real time. Two to four children: take turns as searcher, so each child makes the four searches, and use different codes for each turn. Add the times of the group and use the middle one. Before each timed search, shuffle the 30 antibody cards face up so the child cannot remember where a card lies.
flow.context: In this step you make the cards for the game.

flow.do: 1. Germ 1 arrives for the first time. The helper shows the card and starts the stopwatch. 2. Find the matching antibody card. 3. Stop the watch and write the time. 4. Put the matching card in a separate memory pile. 5. Germ 1 arrives again. Search the memory pile first. Write that time too.
flow.say: A germ arrives for the first time. Find the match as fast as you can. Now the same germ arrives again. Where will you look first?
flow.kid: Germ 1 arrives. Find the match. Time it. Now Germ 1 arrives again. Time it.

check.q: Why is the second meeting with Germ 1 so much faster than the first?
options: The matching card is already in the memory pile
The germ card got easier
You got tired of searching
check.why: The body does the same. After the first meeting, memory cells keep the match ready, so the second time the body finds it at once. The germ card was exactly the same, and you were not more tired.

flow.context: In this step you time the first and second meeting with a germ.

flow.do: 1. The helper shows Germ 2 as a safe picture, which stands for a vaccine. Find the match with no timing and put it in the memory pile. 2. Germ 3 arrives for the first time, with no vaccine. Time the search. 3. Germ 2 arrives for real. Time the search. 4. Write both times.
flow.say: The helper shows you a safe picture of Germ 2. That is the vaccine. You find the match and keep it safe. Now two germs arrive for real, Germ 3 with no warning and Germ 2 after the vaccine. Which will you find faster?
flow.kid: A safe picture of Germ 2 is a vaccine. Find the match. Then time Germ 3 and Germ 2.
flow.parent: Expect the search for Germ 3 to take as long as for Germ 1, often 15 to 30 seconds. The search for Germ 2 after the vaccine takes a second or two. Your child's times will differ, and that is fine. The real body does not read codes; it keeps special cells that already know the germ, and this game only shows how having them saves time.
flow.context: In this step you play the vaccine round and time the two real germs.

flow.do: 1. Draw a bar for each of the four times. 2. Look at the bars together. 3. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Which bar is tallest? Which are shortest? What did the vaccine do? What do you think happened? What did you see? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw four bars. Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: What did the safe picture give your search?
good: It let me find the match before the germ came, so I could look in the memory pile.
It saved time when the real germ arrived.

ask.q: In real life, why is it better to learn the match from a vaccine than from the real germ?
good: With the real germ, the person is ill while the body searches.
The vaccine is safe, so the body can learn without getting ill.

flow.context: In this step you draw the bars and say what the times show.

activities.title: The Vaccine Card Detective

materials.item: your child's vaccination card or health record, such as the Mother and Child Protection card
a grown-up, who knows where the card is
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Find the vaccination card. List each vaccine and the illness it protects against. Count the illnesses.

activities.record: A table with two columns: the vaccine, and the illness it protects against.
activities.context: In this activity you read your own vaccination card, and find out which illnesses each vaccine protects against.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up reading a vaccination card on a table, the card showing a row of stamped dates.
setup.caption: 1. Find your vaccination card and read the list.

setup.art: A child's table with the vaccine name on the left and the illness it protects against on the right, joined by arrows.
setup.caption: 2. Write each vaccine and the illness it protects against.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up finds the vaccination card. 2. Ask your child to guess how many illnesses they are protected against.
flow.say: Every child in India gets a card that lists the vaccines they have had. Let's find yours. How many illnesses do you think you are protected against? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Find your vaccination card. Guess how many illnesses it protects against.
flow.parent: If the card cannot be found, ask the doctor, the health centre or the anganwadi. They keep records. If some doses are missing, do not blame anyone, and ask the doctor which are still worth having.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Vaccine Card Detective. You guess before you read.

flow.do: 1. Read the list of vaccines on the card. 2. Match each with the illness it protects against, using the list below. 3. Write each pair in your table. The list: BCG, tuberculosis. Polio drops or injection, polio. Hepatitis B, hepatitis B. Pentavalent, five illnesses including diphtheria, whooping cough and tetanus. Measles and rubella, measles and rubella. Rotavirus, a cause of loose motions. Booster at ten, tetanus and diphtheria.
flow.say: Your card may use short names. Match each one to the illness it prevents. Some vaccines protect against several illnesses at once.
flow.kid: Read each vaccine on the card. Write the illness it protects against.
flow.parent: Cards differ between states and years, and some families choose extra vaccines, such as those for typhoid or chickenpox. Match what your card shows. If a name is not on the list, ask a doctor or look it up with a grown-up. With several children, each child uses their own card or a photo of it, and they compare lists afterwards. Do not post the card online, because it has personal information.

check.q: One vaccine on the card protects against five illnesses at once. How can one needle do that?
options: It holds a safe piece of each of the five germs
It holds one germ that is tough enough to cover the other four
It is a stronger version of the polio drops
check.why: A combined vaccine holds a safe form or piece of each germ, so the body learns all five at once. A single tough germ would not teach the body about the others.

flow.context: In this step you match each vaccine on the card with its illness.

flow.do: 1. Count the different illnesses on your list. 2. Ask your child which ones nobody in the family has seen. 3. Talk about the question below.
flow.say: How many illnesses are you protected against? Was your guess close? Which of them have you never seen anyone in the family have? Why not?
flow.kid: Count the illnesses. Which have you never seen anyone have?

ask.q: Why have you never seen anyone have polio or tetanus?
good: Because most people are vaccinated, so the germs have nowhere to go.
Vaccines have made these illnesses rare.

flow.context: In this step you count the illnesses and ask why they are rarely seen.

activities.title: ORS: make it, taste it, and see why it works

materials.item: 1 litre of clean drinking water that has been boiled and cooled
6 level teaspoons of sugar (about 30 grams, using a flat-topped teaspoon)
half a level teaspoon of salt
a clean jug, 3 clean cups and a clean spoon for each cup
a packet of ORS from a chemist, to compare, if you have one
paper and a pencil, and a marker or tape to label the cups under the cup base

activities.safety: A grown-up boils the water and lets it cool. Measure the salt and sugar exactly, because too much salt can harm. Taste only a small sip from each cup. This home recipe is for tasting and learning. For a child who is really ill, use a packet of ORS from a chemist or health centre and ask a doctor. Throw away any ORS that is more than a day old.

schedule.what: Make ORS from sugar, salt and clean water. Taste three cups. Think about why ORS has both salt and sugar.

activities.record: A table with three rows: plain water, sugar water and ORS. Write what each tastes like.
activities.context: In this activity you make oral rehydration solution at home and taste it next to plain water and sugar water. You find out why it needs both salt and sugar.

setup.art: A measuring spoon of sugar and a half-spoon of salt beside a jug of clear water on a kitchen counter.
setup.caption: 1. Measure 6 teaspoons of sugar and half a teaspoon of salt.

setup.art: Three small cups in a row labelled plain water, sugar water and ORS, with a child taking a small sip from one.
setup.caption: 2. Stir them in, then taste three cups side by side.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up boils 1 litre of water and lets it cool. 2. Wash your hands with soap. 3. Ask your child to guess what ORS will taste like.
flow.say: When someone has loose motions, the body loses water and salts. A drink of water, salt and sugar puts them back. What do you think it will taste like? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Boil water and let it cool. Wash your hands. Guess what ORS tastes like.
flow.context: This is the first step of the ORS activity. You guess before you taste.

flow.do: 1. Pour the cooled water into the clean jug. 2. Add 6 level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt. 3. Stir until both have dissolved. 4. Pour a little plain water into one cup, and a little of the mixture into another.
flow.say: Six teaspoons of sugar and half a teaspoon of salt in one litre of clean water. Measure them level, not heaped. Too much salt is not safe.
flow.kid: Mix 6 spoons of sugar and half a spoon of salt in the water. Stir well.
flow.parent: Make a third cup of plain sugar water by stirring one level teaspoon of sugar into a cup of the cooled water, with no salt. Keep the jug covered and throw away anything left after a day.

check.q: Why must the salt and sugar be measured exactly?
options: Too much salt can harm, and too little will not replace what the body lost
Because the cups are small
Because the recipe is a secret
check.why: ORS works only in the right balance. Too much salt can make the body lose more water. Too little will not replace what was lost. The balance has been tested in many places.

flow.context: In this step you mix the ORS and measure the amounts exactly.

flow.do: 1. Ask a grown-up to hide the cup labels and mix the order of the cups. 2. Take a small sip from each cup. Use a clean spoon for each. 3. Guess which is plain water, sugar water and ORS. 4. Write how each tastes and check the guesses. 5. If you have a packet of ORS, make a cup of it and compare.
flow.say: Take a small sip of each. Which tastes sweet? Which tastes a little salty? ORS tastes slightly salty, about as salty as tears.
flow.kid: Take a small sip from each cup. Write how each tastes.
flow.context: In this step you taste the three cups.

flow.do: Talk about why ORS has both salt and sugar, and how it is given to a child who is ill.
flow.say: In the gut, sugar and salt are taken into the body together, and water follows them. Without the sugar, much less salt and water get in. A child with loose motions takes small sips every few minutes, even if she vomits. If she cannot keep it down, she needs a doctor.
flow.kid: Sugar and salt go in together, and water follows. Small sips every few minutes help.

ask.q: Why does ORS include sugar if the body is losing salt?
good: The sugar helps the gut take in salt and water together.
Salt and sugar carry the water into the body.

flow.think: ORS does not kill the germ. How does it save a life?
flow.context: In this step you find out why ORS has both salt and sugar.
flow.parent: The home ORS should taste only a little salty, less than tears. If it tastes as salty as the sea, the salt was too much: throw it away and make it again with a level half teaspoon. With a packet, follow the amount of water printed on the packet and not this recipe. One child with a parent: the parent hides the labels. Two to four children: one makes the mixture, one pours, one hides the labels, and all taste and guess.

activities.title: A Day of Temperatures: what is a fever?

materials.item: a digital thermometer. Borrow one from a neighbour or a health worker, or buy one at a medical shop for roughly Rs 100 to 200.
a notebook and a pencil
two family members who are well and agree to be measured. If you have more children, measure each of them too.
a clock

activities.safety: Use a digital thermometer only, never a glass one that can break. Clean the thermometer with soap and water or a cotton ball with a little rubbing alcohol, kept by a grown-up, before and after each use.

schedule.what: Read the thermometer. Take the temperature of two well people in the morning, afternoon and evening. Draw the line.

activities.record: A table with three times for each person, and a line drawing of the readings across the day.
activities.context: In this activity you take the temperature of two well people three times in one day, and find out what a normal temperature looks like before you find out what a fever is.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: one child's temperature over a day

setup.art: A child holding a digital thermometer under the arm of a seated grown-up, reading the screen after the beep.
setup.caption: 1. Place the thermometer in the armpit until it beeps.

setup.art: A notebook with a table of three times and two names, and temperatures written in each cell.
setup.caption: 2. Write down each temperature, three times in one day.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the thermometer and switch it on. 2. A grown-up cleans the tip. 3. Place the tip in the middle of the armpit and hold the arm down against the body until the beep. 4. Read the number and write it down.
flow.say: A body's temperature is about 37 degrees Celsius. Is it exactly 37 all day? Guess. Then we will measure the same two people in the morning, afternoon and evening.
flow.kid: Put the thermometer in the armpit. Wait for the beep. Read the number.

ask.q: Do you think a well person's temperature stays exactly the same all day?
good: Yes, it is always 37.
No, it changes a little.

flow.context: This is the first step of A Day of Temperatures. You learn to read a thermometer.

flow.do: 1. Take the temperature of two well people in the morning. 2. Take it again in the afternoon. 3. Take it again in the evening. 4. Write every reading in the table.
flow.say: Take each person's temperature three times today. The armpit gives a slightly lower number than the mouth. Use the same place every time.
flow.kid: Measure two people three times today. Write each number.
flow.parent: Most well people read between about 36 and 37.5 degrees under the arm. The numbers are usually lowest in the early morning and highest in the late afternoon or evening. The difference is often half a degree or more. Do not take the temperature right after a hot meal, a bath or running. To see how much the thermometer itself varies, take each person's temperature twice in a row at one time of day, and compare the two readings. They often differ by about 0.1 degrees, which is smaller than the change across the day. In hot weather, rest for five minutes in the shade first. Two to four children: each child is measured and also measures the others, and each has a line in a different colour.

check.q: A well person reads 36.4 in the morning and 37.0 in the evening. What does this show?
options: Normal temperature goes up and down a little during the day
The person has a fever in the evening
The thermometer is broken
check.why: A body's temperature is not a fixed number. It is lowest in the early morning and a little higher later in the day. A fever is a temperature clearly above the person's usual range, about 38 degrees or more.

flow.context: In this step you take the temperatures three times in one day.

flow.do: 1. Draw a line through the three readings for each person. 2. Look at the pattern. 3. Talk about the question below.
flow.say: Your readings go up and down a little in a day. A fever is a temperature of about 38 degrees or more. Why do you think the brain raises the body's temperature when germs get in?
flow.kid: Draw a line through the three readings. Does it go up and down?

ask.q: Why might the body raise its temperature when germs get in?
good: It may help the defenders work better.
Some germs grow worse when it is warmer.

flow.think: Scientists are still studying how much a fever helps. What would you test to find out?
flow.context: In this step you draw the line and think about what a fever is for.

activities.title: Ask an Elder: illnesses that went away

materials.item: a grandparent, great-aunt, neighbour or teacher who is happy to talk about illnesses they remember
a notebook and a pencil

schedule.what: Write five questions. Ask an elder about illnesses they remember. Write down the answers and compare with today.

activities.record: A page with the elder's name, five answers, and a list of illnesses that were common then and are rare now.
activities.context: In this activity you interview an older person about illnesses they remember, and compare their answers with what you know about vaccines and clean water.

setup.art: A child with a notebook sitting beside an old woman on a verandah, listening to her.
setup.caption: 1. Write five questions, and ask an elder.

setup.art: A notebook page with two columns, headed then and now, with small pictures of illnesses in each.
setup.caption: 2. Write what you learn, then compare it with today.

flow.do: 1. Choose an elder to ask. 2. Write five questions with your child. For example: Which illnesses did children get when you were small? Which ones frightened people? What did the doctor or the village do? 3. Ask your child what they expect to hear.
flow.say: Let's ask someone who remembers when there were fewer vaccines. What illnesses do you think they remember? What do you think was different?
flow.kid: Write five questions for an elder. Guess what they will say.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ask an Elder. You plan your questions.
flow.parent: If the elder lives far away, the talk can be on the phone or a video call. With several children, each asks one of the questions and writes down that answer.

flow.do: 1. Sit with the elder. 2. Ask each question and listen. 3. Write down the answers. 4. Ask whether they have a scar from a vaccine on their upper arm.
flow.say: Ask your questions one at a time. Listen carefully and write what they say. Do not interrupt. Ask if you may see the vaccine scar on the upper arm, if they have one.
flow.kid: Ask your questions. Listen. Write the answers.
flow.parent: Many older people remember smallpox, polio, measles, whooping cough and cholera, and some have a round smallpox scar on the upper arm. If the elder has sad memories, let them choose what to share. This is a good time for listening.
flow.context: In this step you interview the elder.

flow.do: 1. Look at your answers. 2. Make two columns, then and now. 3. Write which illnesses were common then and are rare now. 4. Talk about why.
flow.say: Which illnesses did your elder talk about that we hardly see today? What changed? Think about vaccines, clean water, toilets and medicines.
flow.kid: Make two columns, then and now. Which illnesses are rarer now? Why?

ask.q: Which changes do you think made the biggest difference?
good: Vaccines.
Clean water and toilets.
Medicines like antibiotics.

flow.think: Was it one thing that changed, or many things together?
flow.context: In this step you compare illnesses then and now.

projects.title: Ask the Health Worker: a one-page health sheet for our home

materials.item: a sheet of chart paper or plain A4 paper
sketch pens or crayons
a notebook for your questions
the family's vaccination cards, if you have them

projects.safety: A grown-up comes to the health centre or the doctor, and chooses what personal information to share. Never write medicine doses on the sheet unless the doctor tells you to. Keep the sheet on the fridge, not in a place children can reach medicines.

schedule.what: Write questions for a health worker, a nurse or a doctor. Plan the layout of the sheet.
Meet the health worker or doctor with a grown-up. Fill in the answers and ask them to check the sheet.

projects.record: A photo or the finished sheet with: the nearest health centre and doctor's number, when the next vaccines are due, the danger signs that need a doctor at once, and how to make ORS.
projects.context: In this 2-day project you ask a real health worker, nurse or doctor your questions, and make a one-page health sheet for your home.

setup.art: A child writing questions in a notebook beside a drawing of a one-page sheet divided into four boxes.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: write your questions and plan the four boxes of the sheet.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up talking to a health worker at a health centre desk, the child writing the answers on a sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: ask the health worker, fill in the sheet and ask them to check it.

flow.do: 1. Divide the sheet into four boxes. 2. Call them: where to go, when to go, vaccines due, and ORS. 3. Write three questions for each box. 4. Choose who to ask: an ASHA worker, an anganwadi worker, a school nurse, a doctor or a pharmacist.
flow.say: A good sheet answers four questions. Where do we go for help? When must we go straight away? Which vaccines are due? How do we make ORS? What questions will you ask?
flow.kid: Draw four boxes on a sheet. Write three questions for each box.

ask.q: Why is it a good idea to ask a real health worker and not only to look things up?
good: They know our area and what is available nearby.
They can check that what we wrote is right.

flow.context: This is the first day of a 2-day project. You plan your questions and your sheet.

flow.do: 1. With a grown-up, meet the health worker, nurse or doctor. 2. Ask your questions and write the answers in the boxes. 3. Ask them to read the sheet and correct anything wrong. 4. Put the sheet on the fridge at home.
flow.say: Say who you are and why you are asking. Write what they tell you, and ask them to check the sheet at the end. A health worker likes a child who asks.
flow.kid: Ask your questions. Write the answers. Ask them to check your sheet.
flow.parent: If you cannot meet anyone in person, call the nearest health centre, or ask the family doctor on the phone. Make sure the doctor's number on the sheet is the right one, and add the number for emergency help: 112 is the national emergency number, and 108 is the ambulance number in most states. With several children, each child owns one box on the sheet and writes the answers for it.
flow.wait: Day 2: meet the health worker or doctor.
flow.context: This is the second day of the project. You ask a real health worker and finish the sheet.

challenges.title: The Vaccine Carrier: keep an ice cube cold for two hours
challenges.problem: Many vaccines must be kept cold, between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius, all the way from the factory to the village. Design a box from things at home that keeps one ice cube from melting for two hours in a warm room.
constraints: Use only things from home, such as a tiffin box, a thermocol box, newspaper, foil, cloth or a cardboard box.
Use an ice cube of the same size in every box, from the same ice tray.
The ice cube must sit in a small steel katori or a plastic cup so the melted water stays in one place.
Keep the lid closed for the whole two hours, and do not put the box in the sun.
challenges.safety: A grown-up cuts any cardboard or thermocol with a knife or scissors. Ice can hurt bare skin if held for long, so pick it up with a spoon or a cloth. Do not put the boxes in the sun or near the stove.
materials: an ice tray with cubes of the same size
a small steel katori or plastic cup for each box
three or more boxes or containers, such as a steel tiffin, a thermocol box or a cardboard box
newspaper, a cloth, aluminium foil, or an old towel to wrap and fill gaps
a measuring spoon or a small cup to measure the melted water
general: Wrap the box in thick layers of newspaper and cloth, which trap air and slow the heat coming in.
Fill the space around the katori with crumpled newspaper so there is no big air gap.
Use a thermocol box, which is a good insulator and light to carry.
creative: Put the katori in a small box inside a bigger box, with newspaper between, for two walls of insulation.
Line the inside with foil with the shiny side in, and wrap the outside in a thick towel.
Add a second ice cube beside the first as an ice pack, and measure only the first.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design. Build it and test it with an ice cube for two hours. Measure the melted water. Change one thing, such as the thickness of the wrapping, and test again. Which design kept the ice longest, and why?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about keeping things cold, as health workers do when they carry vaccines to villages. You build the best cold box you can.

setup.art: A child sketching three cold-box designs on paper: a tiffin with newspaper, a thermocol box and a box inside a box.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some designs on paper.

setup.art: Three boxes in a row, each holding one ice cube in a steel katori, with the lids closed and a clock beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Build them, put one ice cube in each, and start the clock.

setup.art: A child pouring the melted water from each katori into a measuring spoon to compare how much melted.
setup.caption: 3. After two hours, measure the melted water from each.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to sketch two or three designs.
flow.say: A vaccine can spoil if it gets warm. Health workers carry it in a special cold box. How could you keep one ice cube from melting for two hours? Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: Draw two or three ideas for a cold box.

good: Heat coming in from the warm air.
Heat coming in through the sides of the box.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Vaccine Carrier challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Build each box with the things you chose. Put one ice cube in a katori, put the katori inside the box, and close the lid. Write the start time. Make one box a plain tiffin with no wrapping as the comparison.
flow.say: Put an ice cube of the same size in every box. Close the lid. Write the time. The plain box with no wrapping shows us how much the wrapping helps.
flow.kid: Build your boxes. Put an ice cube in each. Close the lids. Write the time.
flow.parent: Take the ice cubes out of the tray at the last moment. Use cubes of the same size. Keep the boxes in the same shady place in the room.
flow.context: In this step you build the boxes and start the test.

flow.do: After two hours, take each katori out. Pour the melted water into a measuring spoon or a small cup. Write how much melted in each box.
flow.say: Pour the melted water from each katori into the same spoon. The box with the least water kept the ice the best.
flow.kid: Pour out the melted water from each katori. Measure it. Write the numbers.

check.q: One box kept the ice cube from melting better than the others. What probably made the difference?
options: It slowed the heat from the room getting in
It made the ice colder
It kept the light out
check.why: Ice melts because heat from the warm room flows into it. A good box slows that heat with trapped air or thick layers. It cannot make the ice colder than it was. Light does not melt ice.

flow.context: In this step you measure the melted water from each box.

flow.do: Talk about what to change and test again if you have time.
flow.say: Which box was best? Which part of the design helped? What would you change? Why does a cold box matter for a vaccine?
flow.kid: Which box was best? What would you change?

ask.q: Why do vaccines need to be kept cold on the way to a village?
good: Heat can spoil the vaccine so it no longer teaches the body.
The vaccine is made of fragile pieces of germs.

flow.context: In this step you talk about your design.

challenges.title: The Medicine Reminder Chart
challenges.problem: Design a chart that helps a grandparent take the right medicine at the right time, using only what the doctor's label says. The chart must be easy to read from one metre away and must be impossible to mix up.
constraints: Copy only what the doctor's label and the pharmacist say, and never change a dose or a time.
The chart must be readable from one metre away by someone who does not read small print.
A grown-up checks the finished chart against every label.
Use things from home such as chart paper, pens and tape.
materials: bold pens in three or four colours
a real medicine label or a made-up one, checked by a grown-up
general: A table with the medicine name down the side and morning, afternoon and night across the top, with a tick box in each cell.
Different colours for morning, afternoon and night.
Big, bold letters, with a picture of a sun, a plate or a moon for each time.
creative: A row of pockets, one for each time of day, with the tablets for that time put in by a grown-up.
A chart with a sticker for each day, so the person can see at a glance what has been taken.
A chart with a picture of what each medicine is for, in a few words, so it is not just a name.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own medicine reminder chart. Draw it, make it, and ask an elder to read it from one metre away. What did they find hard? What did you change?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about doses and times. You make a chart that helps someone take the right medicine at the right time.

setup.art: A medicine label on a bottle lying beside a sheet of chart paper with a table drawn on it.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the label and plan the table.

setup.art: A grandmother reading a large coloured chart stuck on the wall from a metre away, a child watching.
setup.caption: 2. Test the chart. Can an elder read it from a metre away?

flow.do: A grown-up reads a real medicine label with your child. Look for the name, the dose, the times and how long to take it. Write the times in a list.
flow.say: A medicine label tells us the name, how much, how often and for how long. A mix-up can be dangerous. Why do you think a chart helps?
flow.kid: A grown-up reads the label with you. Write down the times.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Medicine Reminder Chart. You read a real label.

flow.do: Sketch two chart designs on paper.
flow.say: Draw two ways to show which medicine goes at which time. How will a person who reads slowly know at a glance?
flow.kid: Draw two ideas. Use colours and pictures.

flow.do: Make the best chart on the chart paper. A grown-up checks it against every label. Then ask an elder to read it from one metre away.
flow.say: Make your chart. Then a grown-up checks it, line by line, with the label. Last, ask an elder to read it from a metre away. What do they find hard?
flow.kid: Make the chart. A grown-up checks it. An elder reads it.

check.q: Why must a grown-up check the chart against the doctor's label?
options: A small copying mistake in a dose or time could harm the person
Because grown-ups are better at drawing
So the chart looks neat
check.why: A dose is chosen for the person and the illness. If a number is copied wrongly, the person may take too much or too little. The chart is a helper, and the label and the doctor are the authority.

flow.do: Talk about what to change.
flow.say: What did the elder find hard to read? What would you change? What other things at home could use a chart like this?
flow.kid: What was hard to read? What would you change?

items.p: Which of these illnesses is NOT caused by a germ?
opts: Measles
Diabetes
Ringworm
Typhoid
items.why: Measles is caused by a virus, ringworm by a fungus and typhoid by bacteria. Diabetes comes from the way the body handles sugar, so nobody can catch it.

items.p: Sort each illness by its cause.
items.a: see items
items.why: Each cause needs a different medicine. Typhoid, tuberculosis and tetanus come from bacteria. Colds and measles come from viruses. Ringworm comes from a fungus. A broken arm and anaemia have no germ at all.

items.p: A medicine that kills bacteria also kills viruses.
items.why: False. Antibiotics attack parts that bacteria have, such as a cell wall, and viruses do not have those parts.

items.p: The time between germs getting in and the first sign of illness is called the ________ period.
items.why: During the incubation period the germs are multiplying, and the person usually feels well.

items.p: Match each medicine to what it does.
pairs: Kills bacteria or stops them multiplying
Replaces water and salts lost in loose motions
Eases fever and pain but does not kill the germ
Teaches the body before the germ arrives
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Medicines do different jobs. Only some of them act on the germ. Others replace what the body has lost, ease signs or prevent illness.

items.p: A child has a runny nose and a mild cough for two days. What is the best help?
opts: Rest and warm drinks
An antibiotic, to be safe
Tablets left over from last time
items.why: A cold is caused by a virus, and the defenders clear it in about a week. An antibiotic does nothing to a virus, and left-over tablets may be the wrong medicine.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last, to show what happens in a body with an infection.
items: The person feels hot and tired
Germs get in and begin to multiply
Antibodies clear the germs and the person gets better
The person feels well for a day or two
Defenders send alarm signals and the temperature rises
a: Germs get in and begin to multiply
The person feels well for a day or two
Defenders send alarm signals and the temperature rises
The person feels hot and tired
Antibodies clear the germs and the person gets better
items.why: The germs multiply quietly first. Then the alarm signals raise the temperature and make the person tired. Last, the antibodies clear the germs.

items.p: A person who takes many antibiotics becomes resistant to them.
items.why: False. It is the bacteria that become resistant, not the person. Tough bacteria survive and multiply.

items.p: Why is the body usually faster the second time it meets the same germ?
items.a: A strong answer says that after the first meeting some white blood cells stay on as memory cells. They remember the shape of the germ and make the right antibody quickly, often before the person feels ill.
items.why: Memory cells are why most people do not get chickenpox twice. A vaccine uses the same trick, so the first meeting is safe.

items.p: A vaccine is made from a killed germ. Why does it not make you ill?
opts: A killed germ cannot multiply, but the body still learns its shape
The vaccine is only water
The body is too strong to be ill
items.why: A killed germ is only a shape for the defenders to look at. It cannot multiply or make a poison. The vaccine is not water, and the body learns because the shape is real.

items.p: A tiny protein that fits one germ, like a key fits a lock, is called an ________.
items.why: An antibody fits one particular germ, sticks to them and marks them to be removed.

items.p: Draw nine houses in a square, three rows of three. Colour one house red for an ill house. Then colour the neighbours of that house to show vaccinated houses, and show where the illness is stopped.
items.a: A drawing in which the vaccinated houses surround the ill house, and arrows from the ill house are stopped at them.
items.why: This is a ring. A germ spreads only to the neighbours within reach, so a ring of protected houses leaves it nowhere to go.

items.p: Which of these is a danger sign that needs a doctor at once?
opts: A child cannot drink and is very sleepy
A runny nose for two days
A child sneezing in the morning
items.why: Not being able to drink and being very sleepy can mean the body is in trouble. A runny nose and a few sneezes are common in a cold.

items.p: Left-over tablets from last month are safe to give for a new illness.
items.why: False. A new illness may have a different cause. The packet may be the wrong dose or the wrong medicine, and it may be out of date.

items.p: Meera has a cold and a sore throat. Her doctor says no antibiotic is needed.

views.says: I want an antibiotic. It will make me better faster, and my friend got one when she had a cold.
The doctor is right. A cold is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not work on viruses.

items.ask: Who do you agree with, and why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with the doctor and Farhan: antibiotics do not work on viruses, and they can leave tough bacteria behind. It also says that Meera is right to want to get better, and that rest and drinks are the real help. If the throat gets worse, the doctor can test for bacteria.
items.why: Wanting to get better is reasonable. The best help is the one that matches the cause.

items.p: ORS has no germ-killer in it. How does it still save the lives of children with loose motions?
items.a: Loose motions make the body lose water and salts. ORS puts them back, so the body does not dry out while the defenders clear the germs.
items.why: Many children die of losing water, not from the germ. Keeping the body topped up gives the defenders time.

items.p: Almost everyone in a school is vaccinated against measles. A baby in the neighbourhood is too young for the vaccine. Why is the baby safer?
opts: The germ keeps meeting protected people and rarely reaches the baby
Babies have a stronger body than children
Measles cannot infect babies
items.why: Each vaccinated person is a broken link in the chain, so the germ has a hard time reaching anyone. Babies can catch measles, and they can become very ill.

items.p: Penicillin weakens the wall of a bacterium so that she bursts. Why does penicillin not harm the cells of a human?
opts: Human cells have no wall for the medicine to weaken
Human cells are bigger
The medicine is washed out by the stomach
items.why: A medicine that attacks a wall has nothing to attack in a human cell, which has no wall. This is how an antibiotic can hurt a germ and leave you alone.

items.p: Taking an antibiotic for a cold can make the cold virus resistant.
items.why: False. An antibiotic does nothing to a virus, so the virus cannot become resistant to the antibiotic. But the antibiotic can still leave tough bacteria behind in the body.

items.p: Two plates start the same, with 38 ordinary germs and 2 tough germs. Plate A gets a medicine every day that removes 9 out of every 10 ordinary germs. Plate B gets none. After two days, which describes Plate A best?
opts: Almost no ordinary germs are left, and the tough germs have multiplied
There are more ordinary germs than at the start
The germs are the same as Plate B
items.why: The medicine removes most ordinary germs each day, and the tough ones survive and double each night. Plate B keeps its crowd of ordinary germs, which holds the tough ones back.

items.p: When the germs that survive a medicine are the ones that carry on, this is called natural ________.
items.why: Natural selection means that the living beings who survive and multiply are the ones whose kind carries on. It shaped every living being, and it shapes germs too.

items.p: A child adds salt, vinegar, garlic and turmeric to separate glasses of yeast and measures the foam after 20 minutes. Why must she also set up a glass with nothing added?
items.a: The glass with nothing added shows how much foam yeast makes normally. Without it, she would not know whether the other glasses made more or less foam than usual.
items.why: A comparison glass is a control. Scientists use one so that any change can be put down to the thing they added.

items.p: Which kind of medicine would a doctor choose? Sort each illness.
items: a throat infection confirmed as bacterial
flu in a person at high risk
a chest infection caused by bacteria
a fungus infection of the foot
items.a: see items
items.why: A doctor matches the medicine to the cause. Antibiotics are for bacteria, antifungal medicines for fungi, and an antiviral for a few viruses. For an ordinary cold, no germ-killer helps.

items.p: A flu vaccine is changed every year. What is the best reason?
opts: Flu viruses change a little, so last year's antibodies may not fit this year's virus
The vaccine goes off after a year in the fridge
Flu is a bacterium
items.why: Antibodies fit one shape, like a key in a lock. If the virus changes their shape, the old key may not fit. So each year's vaccine is matched to the viruses that are going around.

items.p: A neighbour says, "Nobody around here gets measles, so my child does not need the vaccine." Using herd protection, explain what she may be missing.
items.a: A strong answer says that measles is rare around there because most children are vaccinated. If many stop being vaccinated, the germ will find enough unprotected children to spread to, and measles will come back.
items.why: Herd protection works only while enough people stay vaccinated. The reason nobody sees measles is the vaccine.

items.p: Herd protection means that people who are not vaccinated can never catch the illness.
items.why: False. Herd protection makes it less likely, because the germ meets fewer people to pass to. It is not a guarantee.

items.p: About 95 out of every 100 people need to be protected to stop measles spreading. In a class of 40, about how many children is that?
items.why: 95 out of 100 is the same as 19 out of 20. A class of 40 is two lots of 20, so 2 times 19 is 38.

items.p: The rabies vaccine can be given after a dog bite and still protect, because the virus travels ________ to the brain.
items.why: The virus takes weeks to reach the brain, so the vaccine has time to teach the body. Even so, a person must get to a doctor at once.

items.p: Doctors disagree about how long a course of antibiotics should be.

views.says: The rule 'always finish the packet' has little evidence. A longer course gives resistant bacteria more chances to appear. Courses should be as short as works.
For some illnesses, such as tuberculosis, a long course is needed to kill every bacterium, and stopping early is dangerous. It depends on the illness.

items.ask: Which view do you find more convincing, and why? What should a family do while the experts still disagree?
items.a: A strong answer sees that both can be true for different illnesses, and that families should follow the doctor who knows the illness and ask when to stop. Families should not set the length themselves.
items.why: There is no single answer for all illnesses. A good response uses the evidence and respects that the doctor has the details of the case.

items.p: Put these in order to show how tough germs take over a body that takes an antibiotic.
items: Most of the germs in the body are now tough
A few germs in the crowd are already tough by chance
The tough germs multiply with plenty of room and food
a: A few germs in the crowd are already tough by chance
The tough germs multiply with plenty of room and food
Most of the germs in the body are now tough
items.why: The tough germs are there first. The medicine removes their competitors. Then they multiply into the space.

items.p: Why can taking an antibiotic cause loose motions?
opts: It kills some of the helpful bacteria in the gut as well
It is made of salt
It makes the body drink too much
items.why: The gut is home to trillions of helpful bacteria. An antibiotic cannot always tell the helpful ones from the harmful ones, so a change in the gut can cause loose motions.

items.p: A bacteriophage attacks only one kind of bacterium. Give one reason this could be good for a medicine and one reason it could be hard.
items.a: Good: it leaves the helpful bacteria and the person's cells alone. Hard: a doctor must find out exactly which bacterium causes the infection, and must have the right phage ready.
items.why: A narrow tool does less harm but needs more knowledge to use. That is one reason phages are still being tested.

items.p: Draw how a velvet stamp copies a pattern of dots from one dish of bacteria to two new dishes. Show which dish has the medicine in it.
items.a: A drawing of a dish with dots, a round velvet pad pressed on it, then pressed on two new dishes where the same pattern of dots appears, one with a label for the medicine.
items.why: The stamp copies the position of each colony, so scientists can compare the same colony on a dish with and without the medicine.

items.p: A doctor says a throat infection needs an antibiotic only after a test. Why wait for the test?
opts: A sore throat looks the same whether bacteria or a virus cause the pain
Tests make the medicine stronger
The doctor wants the child to wait
items.why: The cause decides the medicine, and you cannot tell the cause by looking. A test avoids giving an antibiotic that cannot help.

worksheets.title: Thinking Like a Scientist About Medicine (challenge)

items.p: A scientist stamps a dish of bacteria on to new dishes with a medicine in them. Resistant dots grow in the same places on every copy, and those same places on the first dish also hold resistant bacteria. Which finding would have shown that the medicine made the bacteria resistant?
opts: Resistant dots appearing in different places on each copy, and none on the first dish
Resistant dots in the same places on every copy
Every dot on the first dish being resistant
items.why: If the medicine caused the change, the resistant dots would appear at random on each copy and would not be found in the first dish. The same places each time show that they were there already.

items.p: A trial gives a new vaccine to 1,000 children and a dummy injection to another 1,000. In the next year, 5 vaccinated children and 50 dummy children catch the illness. What does this show, and how big is the effect?
items.a: The vaccinated group had far fewer cases, 5 against 50. That is 10 times fewer, or 9 out of 10 fewer cases (90 percent fewer).
items.why: Comparing a group that gets the vaccine with one that does not shows what the vaccine does. 50 minus 5 is 45, and 45 out of 50 is 9 out of 10.

items.p: Why does a trial use a dummy injection for the comparison group?
opts: So that both groups expect the same thing, and any difference comes from the vaccine
Because the vaccine is too expensive
To make the trial longer
items.why: If one group knew they had nothing, they might behave differently, and that could change the result. A dummy keeps everything the same except the vaccine.

items.p: A new vaccine is made, but there is only enough for a few thousand people.

views.says: Give it first to the people most likely to become very ill, such as the very old and children with weak defences.
Give it first to the people who meet the most others, such as bus drivers and teachers, so the germ spreads less.

items.ask: Which plan do you find more convincing, and why? What evidence would help decide?
items.a: A strong answer picks a plan and gives a reason, such as protecting the most vulnerable or breaking the most chains. It names evidence that would decide, such as how much each group spreads the germ and how likely each is to become very ill.
items.why: Both plans protect people in different ways. This is a question about fairness as well as science, and a good answer says what it values.

items.p: A friend says, "My grandmother took antibiotics for years, so her body is resistant now." What is right and what is wrong?
items.a: Wrong: the person does not become resistant. The bacteria in her body can become resistant. Right: taking antibiotics often does make resistant bacteria more likely.
items.why: The word resistant belongs to the germ. Careful words help us think clearly about what is happening.

items.p: Bacteria can pass genes for resistance to other kinds of bacteria.
items.why: True. Bacteria can hand pieces of their genes to each other, even across kinds, so resistance can spread fast.

items.p: In one town, measles cases fall every year for ten years. In the last year, the number of vaccinated children falls too. What should a careful scientist say?
opts: Cases may rise soon, because fewer children are now protected
Measles has gone for good
The vaccine has stopped working
items.why: The fall in cases came from past vaccination. If protection drops now, the chains will have more links again. A careful scientist watches the trend and the cause.

items.p: Alexander Fleming saw a clear ring around a mould on a dish of bacteria. What could a scientist do next to find out whether the mould caused the ring?
items.a: Grow the mould alone, then put some liquid from the mould on fresh dishes of the bacteria and see if rings appear. Also use dishes with no mould liquid as a comparison, and repeat the test.
items.why: A ring next to a mould is a clue, not a proof. A test with the mould's liquid alone, and a comparison dish, tells whether the mould is the cause.

items.p: Which of these protects mainly the person, and which also protects others?
items: taking a painkiller for your own headache
covering your cough with your elbow
a plaster on your own cut
wearing sunglasses on a bright day
items.a: see items
items.why: Some actions protect only you. Actions that stop a germ passing on, like a vaccine, an elbow cough or staying at home, protect everyone down the chain.

items.p: Draw a germ chain for a bacterial illness that spreads through water. Mark three places where clean water, a toilet or a vaccine could break the chain.
items.a: A chain of pictures from an ill person to dirty water to a drinker, with three marked breaks such as a toilet that keeps waste away from the water, boiling or filtering the water, and a vaccine for the next person.
items.why: A chain can be broken in many places. Putting the break far from the first case, as with clean water, protects a whole town.

items.p: Smallpox was wiped out, but the common cold cannot be. What is the main reason?
opts: Smallpox was one virus that lived only in people, and there was a strong vaccine, while colds come from hundreds of viruses
Smallpox was a bacterium
Colds are not caused by germs
items.why: To wipe out a disease you need one germ, a way to find every case and a vaccine that works. Colds have hundreds of different viruses that change, so no single vaccine can stop them.

items.p: In 1980, the world was declared free of ________.
items.why: Smallpox was the first human disease to be wiped out. A world campaign found every case and vaccinated the people around it.

items.p: A hospital finds a bacterium that none of the hospital's antibiotics can kill. Give two things the hospital could do to stop it spreading.
items.a: For example: keep the patients who carry it apart from others, make everyone clean their hands carefully between patients, clean the equipment, and test to find the right medicine and use antibiotics only when needed.
items.why: The germ chain can be broken at many links even when no medicine works. Cleanliness and separation work against resistant germs too.

items.p: A grown-up wants to make ORS stronger for a sick child, so adds extra salt. Why is this a bad idea?
opts: The balance of salt and sugar matters, and too much salt can make things worse
Salt makes the sugar disappear
Salt kills the germs
items.why: ORS works only in the tested balance. Too much salt can pull more water out of the body and strain the child. It is safer to measure exactly or use a packet.

items.p: Is 'fighting germs' a good way to think about health? Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.a: For: some germs do cause serious illness, and medicines and vaccines really do stop them. Against: most microbes are harmless or helpful, including the bacteria in our gut, and strong medicines can harm them too.
items.why: A good answer holds two ideas together. We need protection from a few germs, and we live with many microbes that help us.

quiz.p: Which illness is infectious but NOT contagious?
opts: Tetanus
Measles
Chickenpox
quiz.why: Tetanus is caused by bacteria from soil that get into deep cuts, and nobody catches it from another person. Measles and chickenpox pass from person to person.

quiz.p: During the incubation period, what are the germs doing?
opts: Multiplying quietly while the person feels well
Waiting for a medicine
Leaving the body
quiz.why: In the first days, the germs multiply before the defenders raise the alarm. That is why a person can pass germs on before they feel ill.

opts: Fits one germ like a key in a lock, sticks to them and marks them to be removed
Kills every germ at once
Carries oxygen in the blood
quiz.why: An antibody has a shape that fits one particular germ. It does not kill every germ, and oxygen is carried by red blood cells.

quiz.p: Why does an antibiotic not help against a cold?
opts: A cold is caused by a virus, which has no cell wall for the antibiotic to attack
A cold is too small to feel
Antibiotics only work in the morning
quiz.why: Antibiotics attack parts that bacteria have. A virus is not a cell and has none of those parts.

quiz.p: In a game, a medicine removes 9 out of 10 ordinary germs from a crowd but cannot touch the few tough ones. After several days, what will most of the germs be?
opts: Tough ones
Ordinary ones
The same mix as at the start
quiz.why: The medicine removes the ordinary germs, and the tough ones survive and multiply into the space. The medicine did not make any germ tougher. It only chose which ones carry on.

quiz.p: Who or what becomes resistant to an antibiotic?
opts: The bacteria
The person who takes it
The tablet
quiz.why: Resistance belongs to the germs. A person who takes many antibiotics can carry resistant bacteria, but the person does not become resistant.

quiz.p: Which sign means a child should see a doctor at once?
opts: A child who vomits everything and cannot keep a drink down
A child with a runny nose
A child who feels warm after running
quiz.why: A child who cannot keep any drink down can quickly dry out. A runny nose and feeling warm after exercise are common and not dangerous in themselves.

quiz.p: A doctor says a child's cold needs no antibiotic. What is the best next step?
opts: Rest, drinks, and watching for danger signs
Asking another doctor for an antibiotic
Using tablets left over from an earlier illness
quiz.why: A cold is caused by a virus, and the body clears it with time. An antibiotic cannot help, and old tablets are the wrong medicine.

opts: A safe form or piece of a germ, or a harmless copy of the germ's poison
A full-strength germ
Only vitamins
quiz.why: A vaccine shows the defenders what the germ looks like, without being able to make you ill.

quiz.p: Why is the body faster the second time the same germ arrives?
opts: Memory cells stay behind and make the right antibody quickly
The germ gets weaker with age
The body forgets it was ill
quiz.why: After the first meeting, some white blood cells stay on as memory cells. A vaccine uses this by giving the first meeting safely.

quiz.p: Why is a baby too young for the measles vaccine safer when everyone around her is vaccinated?
opts: The germ keeps meeting protected people and has a hard time reaching her
The vaccine goes through the air to her
Babies cannot catch measles
quiz.why: Every protected person is a broken link in the chain. Babies can catch measles, and the vaccine does not travel through the air.

quiz.p: About how many out of 100 people need to be protected to stop measles spreading?
quiz.why: Measles spreads so easily that one ill child can pass it to 12 to 18 unprotected others. So almost everyone, about 95 out of 100, needs protection.

quiz.p: A glass of yeast with strong salt makes much less foam than a glass with nothing added. What does this show?
opts: Strong salt slows a living microbe
Yeast prefers salt
Salt turns into foam
quiz.why: The only difference between the glasses was the salt, so the salt held the yeast back. Strong salt would also harm our own cells, so it is not a medicine.

applications: A hospital lab grows bacteria from a patient on a dish and puts small paper discs of different antibiotics on top. A clear ring round a disc shows which medicine works, the same clue that Fleming noticed round a mould.
Doctors choose an antibiotic only after finding out the cause, and hospitals keep rules to use antibiotics only when they are needed, so that they keep working.
Health workers carry vaccines to villages in insulated boxes with ice packs, and in cold rooms and fridges at health centres, so that the vaccine stays between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius all the way.
When a case of measles, polio or Ebola is found, health workers find the people around the ill person and vaccinate them, which makes a ring that the germ cannot cross.
ORS packets are kept in anganwadis, health centres and chemists, and given with zinc tablets to children with loose motions.
Scientists in many countries study the flu viruses that are going around each year, and the flu vaccine is made to match them.
Vets and farmers vaccinate cattle, poultry and dogs against illnesses such as rabies, and are asked to use antibiotics on animals only when they are needed.
India is one of the biggest makers of vaccines in the world, and factories in cities such as Pune, Hyderabad and Chennai supply vaccines to many countries.
New medicines and vaccines are tested in stages on volunteers, with a comparison group, before they are approved.
Campaigns such as Pulse Polio and Mission Indradhanush visit homes and schools to reach children who missed their doses.
After a deep cut or a dog bite, doctors decide about a tetanus booster or a rabies vaccine, because each can protect even after the germ has got in.

open_questions.q: Why is there still no vaccine for the common cold, or for some illnesses such as HIV?
open_questions.why_open: A cold is caused by hundreds of kinds of virus, and some germs change quickly or hide from the defenders. Scientists are still looking for ways round this.

open_questions.q: Will we find new antibiotics fast enough to keep ahead of resistant bacteria?
open_questions.why_open: Bacteria multiply quickly and change, and very few new kinds of antibiotic have been found in recent years. Nobody knows who will keep ahead.

open_questions.q: How does the body keep a memory of a germ for decades?
open_questions.why_open: Some memory cells last for years, and the body also makes new ones. Scientists have not fully worked out how the memory stays and how long it lasts for each germ.

open_questions.q: Which illness will be the next to be wiped out from the world?
open_questions.why_open: Polio and a few other illnesses are close, but the last cases are the hardest to find, and nobody knows when they will go.

open_questions.q: Can viruses that kill bacteria, called phages, become a normal medicine?
open_questions.why_open: Phages have been used in a few places for about a hundred years, and are being tested again. Nobody knows yet how widely they will work.

open_questions.q: How much does a fever help the body fight an infection?
open_questions.why_open: Many studies suggest that a higher temperature helps some defenders and slows some germs. Other studies find little difference, and fever is hard to test fairly in people.

ask_kids: Which medicines at home kill a germ, and which only ease a sign?
Why do you think a doctor does not always give an antibiotic?

maths.problem: In the Rice and Dal game, the tough germs on a plate double every night. Starting with 2 tough germs and no limit on room, how many are there after 3 nights? After 6 nights?
maths.answer: 16 tough germs after 3 nights, and 128 after 6 nights.
maths.explain: Doubling 3 times: 2, 4, 8, 16. Doubling 6 times: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. After 3 more nights the number is 8 times larger, because 2 times 2 times 2 is 8.
maths.context: In the Rice and Dal game, you play a plate with medicine every day and watch the tough germs double each night.
maths.why_maths: Doubling shows how fast a few survivors can become the whole crowd once the others are gone.

maths.problem: In the Rice and Dal game, a body holds 998 ordinary germs and 2 tough germs. A medicine keeps 1 in every 10 ordinary germs and all the tough ones. After the medicine, what share of the germs left are tough? After one night of doubling and another dose of medicine, is that share bigger or smaller?
maths.answer: After the medicine, about 100 ordinary germs and 2 tough ones are left, so about 1 in 50 is tough. After one night and another dose, about 20 ordinary and 4 tough are left, so about 1 in 6 is tough. The share is bigger.
maths.explain: 998 divided by 10 is about 100. 2 tough out of 102 germs is about 1 in 50. After doubling there are about 200 ordinary and 4 tough. The medicine keeps 1 in 10 ordinary, which is 20. So 4 tough out of 24 germs is 1 in 6. Each dose raises the share of tough germs.
maths.context: In the Rice and Dal game, the medicine removes most ordinary germs each day and leaves the tough ones.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the share of tough germs before and after each dose shows how a medicine changes the crowd.

maths.problem: In Memory Cards, Kavya took 24 seconds to find the matching antibody the first time, and 3 seconds after a safe picture from a vaccine. How many times faster was she, and how many seconds did the vaccine save?
maths.explain: 24 divided by 3 is 8, so she was 8 times faster. 24 minus 3 is 21 seconds saved.
maths.context: In Memory Cards, you act as the body's defenders and time how long it takes to find the matching antibody card.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the two times says how much faster the second search was, and subtracting says how much time was saved.

maths.problem: In the Yeast Test, the Plain glass had a foam of 18 millimetres. The Salt glass had 1, the Vinegar glass 7, the Garlic glass 10 and the Turmeric glass 16. Which glasses had less than half as much foam as the Plain glass? What fraction of the Plain foam did the Vinegar glass keep?
maths.answer: Salt and Vinegar had less than half. The Vinegar glass kept 7 out of 18 of the foam, which is a little less than half.
maths.explain: Half of 18 is 9. Salt (1) and Vinegar (7) are below 9. Garlic (10) is just above 9. Vinegar kept 7 out of 18 of the foam, and 7 is less than 9.
maths.context: In the Yeast Test, you measure the foam in five glasses after 20 minutes, one with nothing added and four with a kitchen thing added.
maths.why_maths: Comparing each glass with half of the Plain glass is a quick way to say which things really held the microbe back.
